name: Rohingya Famous People
description: An open archive of famous Rohingya people: leaders, writers, poets, scholars, doctors and public servants. Read what each of them did, with dates, places and sources.

people.name: A. F. K. Jilani
people.role: Educator, historian, activist and writer
people.epithet: Documenting the Rohingya's own history
people.summary: A Rohingya educator, historian, political activist and writer from Maungdaw, and a founding member of the Rohingya Students Organization at Rangoon University in 1962. He devoted much of his life to documenting Rohingya history, identity, political rights and persecution, notably in The Rohingyas of Arakan: Their Quest for Justice. He was associated with the Arakan Rohingya National Organisation and took part in international advocacy for Rohingya rights.

timeline.text: Born. He was educated in Maungdaw, Buthidaung, Akyab and Kyaukpyu, and then at Rangoon University.
At Rangoon University, where he was involved in Muslim student activities, he became a founding member of the Rohingya Students Organization.
Worked as a teacher and obtained a law degree.

Wrote and translated historical materials on the Rohingya and Arakan, including The Rohingyas of Arakan: Their Quest for Justice. He worked with Rohingya political organisations, was associated with the Arakan Rohingya National Organisation, and took part in international advocacy for Rohingya rights.
Died.

people.biography:
A. F. K. Jilani was a Rohingya educator, historian, political activist, and writer from Maungdaw, Arakan. He was born in 1940 and was educated in Maungdaw, Buthidaung, Akyab, Kyaukpyu, and Rangoon University. At Rangoon University, he became involved in Muslim student activities and was a founding member of the Rohingya Students Organization in 1962. He later worked as a teacher and obtained a law degree. He also wrote extensively about Rohingya history and identity, including The Rohingyas of Arakan: Their Quest for Justice.

Jilani devoted much of his life to documenting Rohingya history, identity, political rights, and persecution. He wrote and translated historical materials concerning the Rohingya and Arakan and worked with Rohingya political organizations. He was associated with the Arakan Rohingya National Organisation and participated in international advocacy concerning Rohingya rights. His historical writings remain an important part of the Rohingya community's own documentation of its history.

people.name: Abdul Hadi
people.birthplace: Bawli Bazaar (Kyein Chaung), Maungdaw Township, Arakan
people.role: Police inspector
people.epithet: The inspector feared and respected by all communities
people.summary: A police officer born in Bawli Bazaar (Kyein Chaung), Maungdaw Township, respected — and feared — by Rohingya and Rakhine communities alike, and known for enforcing the law regardless of ethnicity or religion. For some thirty years he served at police stations across Arakan, from Mrauk-U and Sittwe to Maungdaw, Buthidaung, Kyauktaw and Ponnagyun, confronting bandits and communist insurgents, often at the risk of his own life.
people.quote: If I cannot recapture the bandit leader Phoe Nyunt Sein within seven days, I will resign from my position.

timeline.text: Born in Bawli Bazaar (Kyein Chaung), Maungdaw Township, after his father, the Mrauk-U landowner U Zaw Baw Muluk, was killed by bandits. He grew up in the family's ancestral hometown of Myo Haung (Mrauk-U).
timeline.note: Learning how his father had died, he resolved to fight lawbreakers.

timeline.text: After Burma gained independence he joined the People's Police Force, qualified as a Criminal Police Officer with CID training at Insein, and became known as U Hadi, Sub-Inspector of Myo Haung Police Station.
Transferred to Sittwe No. 1 Police Station, the Clock Tower station, where he married Daw Aye Sein, also known as Aziza Begum.
Led efforts to keep peace and stability in Maungdaw, then served about seven years in Buthidaung, where his son U Shwe Maung, later a Member of Parliament, was born.
Posted to Kyauktaw, then a "black area", he fought the communist insurgents who repeatedly attacked the station, and led the security for General Saw Phyu at the opening of Saw Phyu Village.

Transferred to Ponnagyun in 1976, he captured the feared bandit leader Phoe Nyunt Sein. When the bandit escaped with a guard's rifle, U Hadi promised to resign unless he caught him again within seven days — and did, after surviving the bandit's attempt to shoot him at the U Raz Taung Pagoda festival.

With officers of the National Intelligence Bureau he arrested a township party chairman and recovered weapons hidden beneath his house, and brought many notorious criminals and insurgents of the period under the law.
Retired from the police and settled at House No. 69, Mayu Road, Buthidaung.
Died at his home in Buthidaung on 19 May, aged 86.

people.biography:
Police Inspector U Hadi was a prominent Rohingya figure who was loved, respected, and highly regarded by both Rohingya and Rakhine communities. He was also the father of U Shwe Maung, a Member of Parliament, and U Khin Maung, a high school teacher. Throughout his life, he devoted himself to serving his country and his people, even at the risk of his own life.

U Hadi was born in 1918 in Bawli Bazaar (Kyein Chaung), Maungdaw Township. His full name was Abdul Hadi. He was the son of U Zaw Baw Muluk, a wealthy landowner from Mrauk-U (formerly known as Myo Haung) and a former trustee of the Sandi Khan Mosque. His father, U Zaw Baw Muluk, was a native of Myo Haung. During the First World War, he was attacked by a group of extremist Rakhine bandits and died from seven sword wounds. Following his death, U Hadi’s mother, together with other family members, temporarily relocated to Bawli Bazaar in Maungdaw. It was there that U Hadi was born. When conditions in the region improved, Abdul Hadi returned with his mother and grandmother to Myo Haung, his family’s ancestral hometown, where they settled again.

Abdul Hadi received his education and grew up in Myo Haung Township. After learning from his grandmother that his father had been killed by Rakhine criminals, he developed a strong determination to combat criminals, lawbreakers, and those engaged in unlawful activities. After Burma gained independence, he joined the People’s Police Force and later became a Criminal Police Officer (CPO), having obtained his CID qualification from Insein. He began his police service at Mrauk-U Police Station and became widely known as U Hadi, the Deputy Security Officer (Sub-Inspector) of Myo Haung Police Station. He was respected and feared by people of all communities, including Rakhine and Rohingya. In 1955, he was transferred from Mrauk-U Police Station to Sittwe No. 1 Police Station, also known as the Clock Tower Police Station. While serving in Sittwe, he met and married Daw Aye Sein, also known as Aziza Begum, the granddaughter of U Hassan Thiri, a wealthy landowner from Khwa Sone in Mrauk-U.

He was subsequently transferred from Sittwe No. 1 Police Station to Maungdaw Myoma Police Station. While serving there, he played a leading role in efforts to maintain peace and stability in the region. He was later transferred to Buthidaung Myoma Police Station. While the family was living in the police quarters in Buthidaung, his son U Shwe Maung, who would later become a Member of Parliament, was born. After serving in Buthidaung for approximately seven years, U Hadi was transferred once again, this time to Kyauktaw Police Station. At that time, Kyauktaw was designated a “black area,” and communist insurgents were actively operating in the region. U Hadi fought resolutely against the communist insurgents. As they frequently attacked the police station, he also had to take on security duties with considerable courage and determination. When General Saw Phyu came to Kyauktaw for the opening ceremony of Saw Phyu Village, U Hadi took the lead in providing security for the General during the event.

In 1976, U Hadi was transferred from Kyauktaw to Ponnagyun Police Station. There were many incidents that demonstrated his courage as a police officer. One such incident occurred one night when a cooperative warehouse near Ponnagyun Market was broken into by a group of bandits led by a notorious bandit leader named Phoe Nyunt Sein. Even police officers were said to fear Phoe Nyunt Sein. He was a tall, heavily built, dark-complexioned man. Police Inspector U Hadi managed to capture him and detained him at the police station. About two days later, however, Phoe Nyunt Sein seized a rifle from a police officer who was on guard duty and escaped. The escape caused U Hadi considerable concern, and the matter became so serious that he faced the possibility of losing his position. U Hadi made a promise to the township police chief: “If I cannot recapture the bandit leader Phoe Nyunt Sein within seven days, I will resign from my position.” Police Inspector U Hadi then set out with three police officers to recapture Phoe Nyunt Sein. The following day, Pho Nyunt Sein learned that U Hadi was attending the festival at U Raz Taung Pagoda. He followed U Hadi to the festival and attempted to shoot him from behind. Fortunately, the firearm failed to discharge, and U Hadi narrowly escaped death. U Hadi immediately turned around and fired three shots from his revolver at Phoe Nyunt Sein, after which he succeeded in apprehending him.

In Ponnagyun, U Hadi also courageously served on the front lines in operations against criminals and communist insurgents. While tracking and pursuing communist insurgents, information was received that weapons had been concealed beneath the house of the township party chairman. Acting on this intelligence, a joint team comprising police officers led by U Hadi and personnel from the NIB (National Intelligence Bureau) arrested the party chairman and successfully recovered the hidden weapons. This operation earned U Hadi considerable recognition and a strong reputation. U Hadi also succeeded in bringing many of the notorious criminals and armed insurgents of that period under the authority of the law, effectively putting an end to their criminal and insurgent activities.

For U Hadi, nothing was more important than upholding the rule of law. He was a courageous officer who stood at the forefront of enforcing the law against those who violated it, regardless of their ethnicity or religion, even when doing so meant risking his own life. Police Inspector U Hadi retired from service in 1978 and moved to House No. 69, Mayu Road, Ward No. 2, Buthidaung. Having devoted his life with courage and dedication to serving his country and his people, U Hadi passed away at the age of 86 on May 19, 2004, at his home in Buthidaung, returning to Allah in accordance with His divine will.

people.name: Abdul Hai
people.role: Rohingya politician and member of Parliament
people.epithet: A Rohingya voice in the BSPP legislature
people.summary: A Rohingya political representative from northern Arakan, also known as U Tun Aung Kyaw, who was elected from Maungdaw to Burma's national legislature in 1978, during the BSPP period. Historical records identify him as the only Rohingya representative elected that year, at a time when Rohingya political participation was becoming increasingly restricted.

timeline.text: Elected from Maungdaw to Burma's legislature, the only Rohingya representative elected that year.
timeline.note: Rohingya representation was later severely restricted, particularly after the 1982 Citizenship Law and the exclusion of Rohingya from later elections.

people.biography:
Abdul Hai, also known as U Tun Aung Kyaw, was a Rohingya political representative from northern Arakan. Historical records identify him as a member of Burma's legislature during the BSPP period. He was elected in 1978 from Maungdaw.

Abdul Hai's importance comes from his representation of the Rohingya population in Burma's national legislature at a time when political participation by Rohingya communities was becoming increasingly restricted. Historical records identify him as the only Rohingya representative elected in the 1978 election, from Maungdaw. Rohingya representation was subsequently severely restricted, particularly after the 1982 Citizenship Law and the exclusion of Rohingya from later elections.

people.name: Abul Khair
people.role: Rohingya politician and member of Parliament for Maungdaw
people.epithet: A Maungdaw voice in Burma's Union Parliament
people.summary: A Rohingya politician from Maungdaw, born in 1919, who was elected to Burma's Union Parliament for Maungdaw during the democratic parliamentary era before the 1962 military coup. He is remembered among the Rohingya leaders who sought political representation and development for their communities, and remained a respected political figure after parliamentary politics were abolished.

timeline.text: Born. He came from Maungdaw, Arakan.
Elected to Burma's Union Parliament representing Maungdaw, during the parliamentary era after independence.
Remained a respected political figure after the military takeover ended parliamentary politics.
Died.

people.biography:
Abul Khair was a Rohingya politician from Maungdaw, Arakan, born in 1919. He became involved in public affairs and national politics during Burma's parliamentary period after independence. He was elected to Burma's Union Parliament representing Maungdaw during the democratic parliamentary era before the 1962 military coup.

As a parliamentarian, Abul Khair represented the population of northern Arakan during a period when Rohingya representatives participated in Burma's national political system. Historical accounts identify him among the Rohingya political leaders who sought political representation and development for their communities before the military takeover in 1962. He remained a respected political figure after parliamentary politics were abolished.

people.name: Aung Aung (Sittwe)
people.birthplace: Chin Pyan Street, Kontan Ward, Sittwe, Arakan
people.role: Writer and human-rights activist
people.epithet: The writer who sacrificed his life for justice
people.summary: Writer, human-rights activist and Islamic scholar (Alim) from Sittwe. Under the pen name Aung Aung (Sittwe) he wrote books and essays exposing the persecution of the Rohingya, became the first Rohingya to translate the Holy Quran into Burmese, and was one of the most-followed Rohingya voices online. He died of COVID-19 in Yangon in 2021.
people.quote: Only those who live for the benefit of others, rather than for their own beliefs, convictions, and desires, are truly human. Being a humane person is more important than prioritizing one's race, religion, or faith.

timeline.text: Born Qasim, also known as Maung Kyaw Thein, at his family home on Chin Pyan Street, Kontan Ward, Sittwe. His father, Maulana Jalaluddin, taught at Noemania School.
Took an MA in History at the University of Yangon and the Alim Fazil degree in Islamic studies, and joined national movements while still a student.

Under the pen name Aung Aung (Sittwe) he wrote books, articles and critical essays on the liberation and rights of the Rohingya, among them the book "We Need Your Help to End the Rohingya Genocide", which he wrote and compiled before his death, and "Irrefutable Rohingya Denial: It Is a Way to Genocide", "Myanmar's Most Senior Indigenous Race, Rohingya, Is Also the World's Most Persecuted" and "Myanmar's Crimes Against Humanity".
Became the first Rohingya to translate the Holy Quran into Burmese, in clear modern prose, and made it free for anyone to read as a mobile app on the Google Play Store.
Spoke up through every means he had for the Karen, Kachin, Shan and other communities facing discrimination in Myanmar, regardless of race, ethnicity or religion.

Ran his own website and blog, wrote for international websites, and was regarded as the Rohingya with the most followers on Twitter. Scholars, journalists and researchers from abroad relied on his help, and many books on the Rohingya cite his work.
During the COVID-19 pandemic he criticised the government on social media for failing to protect the public and to provide enough oxygen.
He and his family contracted COVID-19 in early July. He died at home in Tamwe Township, Yangon, on 18 July, aged 54.
timeline.note: His last wish was that his books be sold to support orphaned children in his hometown of Sittwe.

people.biography:
In accordance with his belief that the interests of his people are his own interests, and the interests of his country are his own, Aung Aung (Sittwe) devoted his entire life to opposing injustice and making sacrifices in the pursuit of justice. Most people know him primarily as a writer and a human rights activist.

His achievements and contributions go far beyond these titles. These are merely the aspects of his life that he has allowed the public to know. There are many other remarkable qualities and accomplishments hidden behind the scenes. One of the most distinctive is that he is also a highly knowledgeable Islamic scholar (Alim). He consistently devoted himself to humanitarian work, considering his efforts to serve humanity not merely as acts of goodwill, but as his personal duty and responsibility.

Aung Aung (Sittwe) was born in 1967 at his family home on Chin Pyan Street, Kontan Ward, Sittwe, Arakan State. His father was Maulana Jalaluddin, a teacher at Noemania School. His birth name was Qasim, also known as Maung Kyaw Thein.

Maung Kyaw Thein received his basic education in Sittwe. From an early age, he was known for his intelligence and deep love for religion. Therefore, while pursuing his secular education, he also studied and acquired religious knowledge simultaneously. He pursued his higher education at the University of Yangon, where he majored in History and obtained a Master of Arts degree (MA in History). He also earned the Alim Fazil degree in Islamic studies.

Driven by his strong sense of nationalism and love for his country, Maung Kyaw Thein became involved in national movements from his student days. He wrote numerous books, articles, and critical essays under the pen name Aung Aung (Sittwe), focusing on the liberation and rights of the Rohingya people. The book We Need Your Help to End the Rohingya Genocide was among the works he wrote and compiled before his death.
- Irrefutable Rohingya Denial: It Is a Way to Genocide
- Myanmar's Most Senior Indigenous Race, Rohingya, Is Also the World's Most Persecuted
- Myanmar's Crimes Against Humanity

Through these publications, he exposed the persecution and suffering endured by the Rohingya people to the international community and sought justice for them.

He did not stand up for the Rohingya people alone. Since 2012, he had also been firmly advocating for justice through every possible means for ethnic communities such as the Karen, Kachin, and Shan, who have faced discrimination, oppression, and the denial of their rights within Myanmar, regardless of their race, ethnicity, or religion.

Furthermore, he also devoted himself to the promotion and development of Islam. One of his most invaluable contributions was translating the Holy Quran into clear, simple, and easily understandable modern Burmese prose. He was also the first Rohingya to translate the Holy Quran into the Burmese language. His dedication and generosity seemed to know no bounds. He made his Burmese translation of the Holy Quran available as a mobile application on the Google Play Store, allowing anyone to download, read, and study it free of charge. He also compiled and published other religious books and literature, striving to guide those who had lost their way towards the right path.

He was also highly active in advocating for the Rohingya cause through popular internet and social media platforms. He could be considered one of the most active Rohingya activists in the online world. He established his own website and blog under the name Aung Aung Sittwe, where he published numerous articles on national issues, the struggle for rights, and standing in solidarity with oppressed communities. He also contributed extensively to international websites. On social media platforms such as Twitter and Facebook, he regularly published articles and shared reliable news and information from inside Myanmar, earning the trust and confidence of his followers. He was even regarded as the Rohingya with the largest number of followers on Twitter.

He also regularly assisted international scholars, media organizations, and researchers with their projects related to the Rohingya issue. Through these contributions, he earned the trust and respect of many international academics and researchers. Numerous books and publications on the Rohingya written by foreign authors also contain references to the work and research of Aung Aung (Sittwe).

During the COVID-19 pandemic, he strongly criticized the Myanmar government on social media, accusing it of neglecting its responsibility to protect and care for the public and failing to provide sufficient oxygen cylinders. He highlighted how people were dying in large numbers along roadsides and in public places due to the lack of essential medical assistance. He also accused the government of using the pandemic as a weapon against its own people.

The pandemic also affected Aung Aung (Sittwe) and his family. On July 5–6, he and all members of his family contracted COVID-19.

Aung Aung's condition became critical on the evening of July 13, when he had to rely on an oxygen supply to breathe. Without access to adequate medical treatment, his health continued to deteriorate day by day, and he never recovered. On July 18, 2021, at 4:40 a.m., the writer passed away at his home on 144th Street, Tamwe Township, Yangon Region, at the age of 54, answering the call of Allah. He left this world without being able to completely free the oppressed Rohingya people from the cycle of persecution and suffering. With his passing, the Rohingya community lost a courageous and dedicated warrior for justice and truth. His final wish was to have his books sold and to use whatever money was raised from their sales to support orphaned children in his hometown of Sittwe. Before his death, he entrusted this final wish to one of his closest friends.


*— Luthu Wunna, 3 April 2023*

people.name: Aung Kyaw Moe
people.role: Deputy Minister for Human Rights, National Unity Government
people.epithet: A Rohingya voice in the National Unity Government
people.summary: Aung Kyaw Moe is a Rohingya politician and human rights advocate from Maungdaw who serves as Deputy Minister for Human Rights in Myanmar's National Unity Government (NUG), the parallel civilian government formed in opposition to the military junta. Appointed on 30 June 2023, he was the first Rohingya person to serve in a ministerial position in the NUG. In 2017 he founded the Center for Social Integrity, a Myanmar-based humanitarian organization that defends the rights of marginalized communities, especially the Rohingya.

timeline.text: Born in Maungdaw, Rakhine State, where he experienced structural discrimination against Rohingya communities from an early age.

Completed a Bachelor's degree in Yangon and later a Master's degree at Deakin University in Australia; he also took part in leadership programs with the United States Institute of Peace and the Dalai Lama Fellowship.
Worked for over 15 years with international NGOs and agencies in countries including Myanmar, Thailand, Afghanistan and Liberia, on human rights, conflict resolution and humanitarian assistance.
Founded the Center for Social Integrity, a humanitarian organization dedicated to building peace, promoting pluralism and defending the rights of marginalized communities, especially the Rohingya.
Shortly after the military coup, he was appointed human rights adviser to the NUG, where he helped shape inclusive policies and advocated for Rohingya inclusion in national political processes.
On 30 June he was appointed Deputy Minister for Human Rights, the first Rohingya person to serve in a ministerial position in the NUG.

Has spoken internationally, including at the University of Toronto, about inclusive democracy, Rohingya rights and a federal, pluralistic Myanmar; he publicly applauded Bangladesh's support for Rohingya refugees.

people.biography:
Aung Kyaw Moe is a Rohingya politician, human rights advocate, and the Deputy Minister for Human Rights in the Myanmar National Unity Government (NUG) — the parallel civilian government formed in opposition to the military junta. He was born in 1983 in Maungdaw, Rakhine State, Myanmar, where he experienced structural discrimination against Rohingya communities from an early age.

He completed a Bachelor’s degree in Yangon and later earned a Master’s degree from Deakin University in Australia. He also participated in leadership programs with the United States Institute of Peace and the Dalai Lama Fellowship, building skills for peace, pluralism, and human rights work.

Aung Kyaw Moe has worked with international NGOs and agencies across multiple countries including Myanmar, Thailand, Afghanistan, and Liberia for over 15 years, focusing on human rights, conflict resolution, and humanitarian assistance.

In 2017, he founded the Center for Social Integrity, a Myanmar-based humanitarian organization dedicated to building peace, promoting pluralism, and defending the rights of marginalized communities, especially Rohingya.

In 2021, shortly after the military coup in Myanmar, Aung Kyaw Moe was appointed human rights adviser to the NUG, where he helped shape inclusive policies and advocated for Rohingya inclusion in national political processes. On 30 June 2023, he was appointed Deputy Minister for Human Rights, making him the first Rohingya person to serve in a ministerial position in the NUG.

He has spoken internationally, including at academic panels such as at the University of Toronto, about inclusive democracy, Rohingya rights, and the need for a federal, pluralistic Myanmar. He publicly applauded Bangladesh’s support for Rohingya refugees and urged their concerns be integrated into Myanmar’s broader democratic movement.

people.name: Aung Zaw Win
people.role: Businessman, politician and member of Parliament
people.epithet: Raising Maungdaw's questions in Parliament
people.summary: A Rohingya businessman and politician who represented Maungdaw in Myanmar's Union Parliament, elected in the 2010 general election and serving in the Upper House during the 2011–2016 parliamentary period. In September 2011 he raised a parliamentary question on the issuing of national registration cards to Maungdaw residents.

timeline.text: Elected in the general election as an Upper House representative for Maungdaw, serving in the Union Parliament from 2011 to 2016.
In September, raised a question in Parliament about issuing national registration cards to Maungdaw residents.
Met local residents in Maungdaw to discuss development and identification issues.

people.biography:
Aung Zaw Win is a Rohingya businessman and politician who served as a member of Myanmar's Parliament representing Maungdaw. He was elected during the 2010 general election and served in the Union Parliament during the 2011–2016 parliamentary period. Contemporary reporting identifies him as an Upper House representative from Maungdaw.

During his parliamentary period, Aung Zaw Win raised issues concerning Maungdaw residents. Parliamentary records cited in academic research show that he raised a question concerning the issuance of national registration cards to Maungdaw residents in September 2011. He also met local residents in Maungdaw and discussed development and identification issues.

people.name: B. A. Jafar
people.birthplace: Ali Yaung (Ale Chaung) Village, Buthidaung Township, Arakan
people.role: Revolutionary leader
people.epithet: An unfading star of the Rohingya resistance
people.summary: A notable leader of the Rohingya resistance movement. Born Mohammed Jafar Habib in Buthidaung Township around 1939, he studied at Rangoon University, co-founded the Rohingya Students Organisation, and turned down a life in the United States to resist General Ne Win's military dictatorship. He helped found the Rohingya Independence Front in 1964, led the Rohingya Patriotic Front from 1973, and worked to bring the persecution of the Rohingya to international attention.
people.quote: To rebel against and resist evil is to obey the command of God.

timeline.text: Born around 1939 in Ali Yaung (Ale Chaung) Village, Buthidaung Township, into a wealthy and well-educated family; his father was Habibuz Zaman.
Represented the Mayu region in the Arakan Muslim Students' Association of Rangoon University. While at university he also worked as a translator at the Egyptian Embassy.

With other Rohingya students he founded the Rohingya Students Organisation (RSO) in March and became its vice-president. That year he earned his B.A. in Philosophy, Political Science and Modern History, and joined the student protests of 7 July.
timeline.note: Two years later he was elected the organisation's president.

timeline.text: On 26 April, after a solemn pledge at the old mosque of Mayong Khali Market, he and fellow patriots took a blood oath and founded the Rohingya Independence Front (RIF), with Saya Gyi Sultan as its leader. It began by resisting the dictatorship through non-violent means.

Declined a promising chance to emigrate to the United States, and travelled to Pakistan as the RIF's representative, where he met President Ayub Khan and presented accounts of discrimination and human-rights violations in Burma.

Concluding that non-violent resistance had not achieved its aims, he and his RIF colleagues joined Jafar Sani's Mujahid Party in armed resistance. To tell the two Jafars apart, he became known as "B. A. Jafar".

Early in the year the Communist Party and the Burmese military jointly launched a surprise attack on the headquarters in Rathedaung; after months of fighting, the resistance forces withdrew from their positions one by one.
After he, Jafar Sani and Mayu Rashid agreed to reorganise and modernise the resistance, the Rohingya Patriotic Front (RPF) was established on 12 September with him as its leader.

Educated young men pledged themselves to the RPF, among them Saya Shabbir Hussein, the lawyer Nurul Islam, Dr. Yunus and Professor Khin Maung — some of whom later led resistance organisations of their own.

During the Nagamin (Dragon King) Operation, which drove large numbers of Rohingya from their homes, he worked to draw the world's attention to the persecution through publications such as "Rohingyas' Outcry and Demands" and "Genocide in Burma Against the Muslims of Arakan", and through reports to international human-rights bodies.

Travelled to Saudi Arabia to meet Muslim leaders from around the world, and on his return reconciled an internal revolt within the RPF. When vice-president Shabbir Hussein later took over the leadership, he rallied the comrades who stayed loyal and reorganised the RPF.
Died of hepatitis on 6 November, still committed to the movement.
timeline.note: His example inspired and nurtured a new generation of Rohingya activists and resistance leaders.

people.biography:
In the history of the Rohingya resistance movement, three prominent leaders bearing the name Jafar emerged, each distinguished by both courage and wisdom. Among them, B. A. Jafar was a notable revolutionary leader. He sought to reform the traditional approach to resistance through new ideas and perspectives, laying the foundation for a modern revolutionary movement. He courageously resisted what he regarded as an oppressive military dictatorship and devoted his entire life to the cause of his people.

B. A. Jafar was born around 1939 in Ali Yaung (Ale Chaung) Village, Buthidaung Township. His full name was Mohammed Jafar Habib, and his father was Habibuz Zaman. He came from a wealthy and well-educated family. His paternal uncle, Ashraf Zaman Chowdhry, was also a prominent and highly respected figure in Buthidaung Township.

Jafar received his basic education in Moni Bil and Buthidaung. He completed his intermediate studies at Notre Dame College in Dhaka, East Pakistan. He then went to Rangoon to pursue higher education and attended Rangoon University, where he studied Philosophy, Political Science, and Modern History, earning a Bachelor of Arts (B.A.) degree in 1962. Jafar actively participated in the student protests of July 7, 1962. He subsequently continued his studies toward a Bachelor of Laws (B.L.) degree. However, before completing the program, he left university and chose the path of resistance against the dictatorship.

While studying at Rangoon University in 1961–62, Jafar was appointed as the representative for the Mayu region in the Arakan Muslim Students’ Association of Rangoon University. In addition, Jafar and other Rohingya students took the initiative to establish the Rohingya Students Organisation (RSO) in March 1962. Jafar became the vice-president of the organization, while Hussein Qasim was elected president. Two years later, when a new election for the presidency was held, Jafar was elected president of the organization, and Saya Shabbir Hussein was appointed vice-president. While studying at Rangoon University, Jafar also worked as a translator at the Egyptian Embassy.

In 1964, Jafar returned to Buthidaung to attend the wedding of his cousin, Abu Sufian. At the wedding, Jafar met Shuna Ali of Dabyu Chaung, Saya Gyi Nazir Ahmad, and Dr. Zahid Hussein. They went to the nearby Sikandar Dargah, where they sat together and discussed the country’s deteriorating situation. They came to a common belief that a resistance movement needed to be initiated in response to the worsening conditions. The following day, they left for Maungdaw to meet and consult with other patriotic figures, including Saya Gyi Sultan. During their discussions, they agreed to resist the military dictatorship by whatever means were available to them. They then travelled to Mayong Khali Market, where they performed the Asr prayer at the old market mosque and made a solemn pledge. On April 26, 1964, they took a blood oath and launched a new phase of the Rohingya resistance movement. The organization was named the Rohingya Independence Front (RIF), and the title given to its leader was “Grand Raja.” Saya Gyi Sultan was chosen as its leader. As Jafar was still relatively young, leadership was entrusted to the respected and experienced elder, Saya Gyi Sultan. The organization initially began its resistance to the military dictatorship through non-violent means. Its stated objectives were to oppose what it regarded as oppressive rule, to work together with other ethnic groups to bring an end to General Ne Win’s authoritarian system, and to restore the rights that the Rohingya people had lost.

After his cousin’s wedding had concluded, Jafar returned to Rangoon. Upon his return, the Burma Socialist Programme Party (BSPP) government banned Urdu-language newspapers, and as a result, Jafar also lost his translation job. The Ministry of Religious Affairs had previously provided 65,000 kyats in financial support to the Muslim Students’ Association, but this funding was subsequently withdrawn by Brigadier General Kyaw Soe. Jafar therefore worked tirelessly alongside Syed Anwar Azim, Vice-President of the Rangoon University Muslim Students’ Association (RUMSA), to secure advertisements and raise funds for RUMSA’s annual magazine. The two shared similar political convictions: both believed in the democratic path and strongly opposed all forms of dictatorship. They also worked persistently to seek the relaxation of government restrictions imposed on Muslim students at Rangoon University.

While Jafar was in Rangoon, he received a promising opportunity to immigrate to the United States. He was also closely acquainted with Dr. Tin Maung, also known as Abul Hussein, a nuclear scientist residing in the United States. When Dr. Tin Maung returned to Rangoon after earning his doctorate, the Rohingya Students Organisation invited him to a formal ceremony held in his honor. In addition, Jafar’s relatives living in the United States invited him to move there and expressed their willingness to provide him with the assistance and financial support he would need. With their support, it would have been relatively easy for Jafar to settle in the United States. However, rather than pursuing what could have been a promising future for himself, Jafar chose to give priority to what he saw as a greater cause: helping his people and his country escape the military dictatorship’s unjust oppression.

After returning from Rangoon, Jafar married his childhood sweetheart and lifelong companion, the daughter of Ashraf Zaman Chowdhry. Subsequently, by decision of the organization, Jafar travelled to Pakistan as a representative of the Rohingya Independence Front (RIF).

He met Pakistani President Ayub Khan and presented accounts of ethnic discrimination and human-rights violations in Burma. He also requested assistance for Burmese citizens involved in opposition to the military dictatorship. Jafar also met General Ziaur Rahman, who would later become President of Bangladesh, and discussed with him allegations of oppression and mistreatment of the population by Ne Win’s government in Burma. He requested that Pakistan exert pressure on Burma’s military government.

After concluding that non-violent resistance against the military dictatorship had not achieved its objectives, Jafar and his RIF colleagues joined Jafar Sani’s Mujahid Party in 1971 and began an armed resistance. Since the leader of the Mujahid Party was also named Jafar Sani, Mohammed Jafar Habib came to be known distinctly as “B. A. Jafar” to avoid confusion between the two men. Under an RIF initiative, Mayu Rashid, also known as Ba Maung, and Molvi Kabir were sent to Thailand to meet and hold discussions with former Prime Minister U Nu, who was then seeking to remove Ne Win from power.

In early 1973, the Communist Party and the Burmese military jointly launched a surprise attack on Jafar’s headquarters in Rathedaung. The Rakhine Communist Party had previously been allied with Jafar Sani. However, it broke the alliance and joined forces with the Burmese military to attack the Mujahid group. The fighting continued for several months, with heavy casualties on both sides. In the initial stages, Jafar’s forces gained the upper hand. Later, however, the Burmese armed forces brought in reinforcements and intensified their offensive. As a result, Jafar’s forces were gradually forced to withdraw, one by one, from the bases and positions they had been holding.

Around the middle of 1973, B. A. Jafar, Jafar Sani, and Mayu Rashid held a three-way discussion and agreed that the time had come to reorganize and modernize the existing resistance movement in accordance with contemporary military strategies.

On September 12, 1973, the Rohingya Patriotic Front (RPF) was established under the leadership of B. A. Jafar, who was appointed as the leader of the organization.

In 1974, several more educated young men pledged their allegiance to Jafar’s organization. Among those who joined were Saya Shabbir Hussein, lawyer Nurul Islam, Dr. Yunus, and Professor Khin Maung, some of whom would later become leaders of resistance organizations themselves.

During the 1978 Nagamin (Dragon King) Operation, when large numbers of Rohingya were forcibly displaced, many young people joined Jafar’s organization, and the Rohingya Patriotic Front (RPF) grew stronger than before. Jafar worked to draw international attention to what he regarded as the intentions of Ne Win’s government behind the 1978 Nagamin Operation. Through publications such as Rohingyas’ Outcry and Demands and Genocide in Burma Against the Muslims of Arakan, he sought to bring international attention to the systematic repression and persecution of the Rohingya and to present their demands to the wider world. He also submitted reports to international human-rights bodies in an effort to seek justice for the Rohingya. In addition, he sent representatives to a World Muslim Conference held in Malaysia.

After 1978, Jafar travelled to Saudi Arabia, where he met with Muslim leaders from around the world, including Muslim leaders from the Philippines. Upon his return from Saudi Arabia, an internal revolt broke out within the Rohingya Patriotic Front (RPF). Jafar, however, succeeded in reconciling and reorganizing those within the movement who had developed disagreements.

As the RPF began to regain its strength, another internal power struggle arose over the leadership of the organization. Vice-President Shabbir Hussein, also known as U Maung Tin, removed Jafar and assumed control of the leadership. Jafar then rallied the comrades who remained loyal to him and reorganized the RPF. He appointed Dalil Ahmad as the military commander.

B. A. Jafar’s selfless involvement in the resistance movement inspired and nurtured a new generation of young activists who would later dedicate, and in some cases sacrifice, their lives for the Rohingya people. His movement also helped produce a new generation of resistance leaders. While striving to realize his dream of the “liberation of the Rohingya people,” Jafar passed away from hepatitis on November 6, 1987, before he could see that dream fulfilled. Until his final breath, B. A. Jafar remained steadfastly committed to the national resistance movement and worked tirelessly for its cause. In the history of the Rohingya resistance movement, B. A. Jafar will forever be remembered as an unfading star whose legacy continues to shine.

people.biography:
Chit Lwin Ebrahim, also known as U Ebrahim, is a prominent Rohingya lawyer, accountant, and politician from Maungdaw, northern Rakhine State, Myanmar. Born in 1946, he earned a Bachelor of Commerce in 1967 and later qualified as a certified accountant and lawyer, practicing at the High Court of Rangoon.

Ebrahim's political career began in the late 1980s as a leading figure in the National Democratic Party for Human Rights (NDPHR), the main Rohingya political party at the time. In the 1990 Myanmar General Election, he contested and won the Maungdaw-1 Constituency with 20,045 votes, becoming one of only four Rohingya Members of Parliament elected nationwide. As Chairman of the NDPHR, Ebrahim worked to promote Rohingya representation, equality, and citizenship rights through peaceful and democratic means. However, the military junta banned the NDPHR and barred its leaders from politics in 1992.

people.role: Royal poet of the Mrauk U court
people.epithet: One of the earliest Bengali poets of the Arakan court
people.summary: A Bengali poet of the royal court of the Mrauk U kingdom in Arakan, born in 1600 in Sultanpur in the Chittagong region, who moved to Arakan seeking recognition for his literary talent. Under the patronage of Ashraf Khan, a Sufi officer of King Thiri Thudhamma, he began Satimayna Lor Chandrani, a Bengali verse adaptation of Avadhi folk narratives, which the poet Alaol completed after his death in 1638.

people.biography:
Daulat Kazi was a distinguished Bengali poet who served in the royal court of the Mrauk U Kingdom (present-day Rakhine State, Myanmar). Born in 1600 in Sultanpur, Chittagong region (now Bangladesh), he moved to Arakan seeking recognition for his literary talent.

Under the patronage of Ashraf Khan, a Sufi officer under King Thiri Thudhamma (reigned 1622–1638), Daulat Kazi began composing Satimayna Lor Chandrani, an adaptation of Avadhi folk narratives into Bengali verse. He passed away in 1638 before completing it, and the work was later finished by the poet Alaol.

Daulat Kazi is remembered as one of the earliest Bengali poets in the Arakan court, contributing to the rich cultural and literary heritage of medieval Arakan. His works represent a significant fusion of Bengali literary traditions and Arakanese patronage.

people.biography:
Daw Zohra Begum, also known as Daw Aye Nyunt, was a pioneering Rohingya politician from Akyab (now Sittwe), Arakan, Myanmar. Born on 10 April 1919 in Rupah Quarter, she was the daughter of U Po Khine, a prominent Rohingya community leader and President of the All Burma Muslim Congress, and Daw Ma Ma. She completed her early education at St. Anne’s Convent and Akyab Government High School, passing the university entrance exam in 1937. She initially pursued pre-medical studies before transferring to a teacher’s college.

In the 1951–52 parliamentary elections, Daw Zohra Begum was elected as Member of Parliament for Maungdaw South, winning over 75% of the vote. She became one of only two women in the Union Parliament—alongside Khin Kyi, and the first female MP from Arakan. Her father, U Po Khine, was elected as MP for Akyab North, and her husband, Sultan Ahmed, was elected from Maungdaw North and served as a parliamentary secretary.

She served in the Union Parliament until 1956, when she lost her seat to Rohingya police officer Abul Khair. Daw Zohra Begum remains celebrated as a trailblazer for women’s political participation in Arakan and a historic representative of the Rohingya community in national politics.

people.name: Dr. Wakar Uddin
people.role: Academic, activist and Director General of the Arakan Rohingya Union
people.epithet: A Rohingya voice on the international stage
people.summary: Dr. Wakar Uddin was a Rohingya academic and activist from Maungdaw, Arakan, who advocated for the rights of the Rohingya people on the international stage. A professor at Pennsylvania State University, he was the founding chairman of the Burmese Rohingya Association of North America and president of Muslim Aid America, and as Director General of the Arakan Rohingya Union (ARU) he engaged the United Nations and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) on Rohingya human rights. He died in Baltimore, Maryland, in 2022.

Several Rohingya organizations issued a joint statement calling for reforms in the ARU leadership, saying some of his actions and decisions did not fully represent Rohingya interests.

people.biography:
Dr. Wakar Uddin was a prominent Rohingya academic and activist dedicated to advocating for the rights of the Rohingya people on the international stage. Born in Maungdaw, Arakan (Rakhine State), Myanmar, he pursued higher education abroad and established himself as a respected scholar.

He earned a doctorate in the United States and served as a professor at Pennsylvania State University. Dr. Uddin was the founding chairman of the Burmese Rohingya Association of North America and president of Muslim Aid America, through which he worked to support Rohingya communities globally.

Dr. Uddin was appointed Director General of the Arakan Rohingya Union (ARU), an organization recognized by the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) as the official representative body of the Rohingya people. In this role, he engaged with international institutions, including the United Nations and OIC, advocating for Rohingya human rights and seeking international intervention against abuses in Myanmar.

Despite his official position, Dr. Uddin faced criticism and opposition from some Rohingya groups. In 2019, multiple Rohingya organizations issued a joint statement calling for reforms in the ARU leadership, expressing concerns that some of his actions and decisions did not fully represent Rohingya interests.

Dr. Wakar Uddin passed away on 29 April 2022 in Baltimore, Maryland, USA, while receiving treatment at Johns Hopkins University Hospital. His death was mourned by Rohingya organizations and activists who acknowledged his efforts to promote peace and social harmony in Arakan.

people.summary: Barrister-at-law, Municipal Commissioner and the leading businessman of colonial-era Sittwe. people.biography:
During the colonial period, one of the most prominent wealthy and educated figures in Sittwe was none other than the wealthy businessman Marakan. He was a native of Sittwe and was a barrister-at-law. His full name was Mr. E. Kader Marakan.

Mr. E. Kader Marakan had served as a Municipal Commissioner of Sittwe since 1906 and was also an Honorary Magistrate. He was a Vice-President of the Arakan Anjuman-i-Islamia and a member of the governing board of Sittwe Government High School. (The Arakan Anjuman-i-Islamia was founded in 1909 by Saya Gyi Miah Abdul Hamid, who served as its president, while T. U. Ahmed, editor-in-chief of The Arakan News, the first newspaper in Arakan, served as its honorary secretary.) Marakan controlled several major commercial enterprises in Sittwe, including cargo handling, general trading, and commission agency businesses. He also owned a large ship as well as fifteen cargo vessels, each capable of carrying between 50 and 60 tons, and more than a thousand employees depended on his businesses for their livelihoods. He established the firm Maracan E. K., Well St., Sub-Agent, Burma Oil Co., through which he secured important government contracts for the transportation of coal and petroleum and exported these commodities abroad. His business associates and representatives included Thomas Brock & Co., 29 Waterloo Street, Glasgow, and Mr. A. J. Ismay, Stoke Newington, London.

The business enterprise later managed by E. Kader Marakan was originally founded by his father, the wealthy businessman Mr. E. S. Maracan, who was a native of Karaikal, Pondicherry, and came to Sittwe around the 1850s. E. S. Maracan was known as a generous philanthropist who contributed extensively to charitable causes. At his own expense, he financed the expansion of the main building of the General Hospital and donated several other buildings. He also constructed and donated an impressive mosque and an English school. Beyond Sittwe, he funded the construction of schools and mosques in other townships as well. He was regarded as one of the leaders of the Muslim community of his time and served for a period as a Municipal Commissioner, contributing to the welfare of the public. Mr. E. S. Maracan passed away in 1960.

After his father’s death, E. Kader Marakan became the administrator of the family estate and succeeded his father in managing the family’s affairs and enterprises. At the time, the property left by his father was valued at more than 300,000 rupees. He transferred the school founded by his father to the Municipal Committee, which later administered and supervised it in association with the local Government High School. In honor of its founder, the school was renamed E. S. Maracan’s Anglo-Vernacular School.

Among the children of E. K. Marakan, two of his sons became prominent figures in Burmese politics: his eldest son, E. G. S. Maracan (Esmail Ghani Shah Maracan), and E. D. S. Maracan (Esmail Dawood Shah Maracan). E. G. S. Maracan was widely known as Gani Maracan (Gani Markin). In 1936, Gani Maracan became a legislative representative for northern Sittwe District. He was also an enthusiastic horseman who bred horses and regularly participated in horse races, in which he also won championships. E. D. S. Maracan, Dawood Shah Maracan, was popularly known as Tanbi Saheb and was one of the leaders who worked to bring an end to the communal violence of 1942. Both brothers were awarded medals associated with King George VI, the father of Queen Elizabeth II.

The Marakan family was exceptionally generous and deeply committed to charitable giving. It is said that the land on which U Ottama Park is located was also donated by the Marakan family. In addition to Sittwe, the family made charitable contributions and owned properties in various other towns and cities across Burma.

people.biography:
Fazal Ahmed is a prominent Rohingya lawyer and former politician from Maungdaw, Arakan. As a senior member and central leader of the National Democratic Party for Human Rights (NDPHR), he was elected as a Member of Parliament (MP-elect) for the Maungdaw-2 constituency in the 1990 general election, becoming one of only four Rohingya MPs to win seats.

Ahmed devoted his professional life to pursuing equality and justice, serving in government offices before qualifying as a Higher Grade Pleader (HGP) and practicing law in Maungdaw. He provided legal support to Rohingya citizens facing discrimination and citizenship denials. As a parliamentarian-elect, he worked to promote the recognition of the Rohingya as an ethnic group of Myanmar and demanded the restoration of their citizenship rights. He advocated for peaceful coexistence between Rakhine Buddhists and Rohingya Muslims.

After the NDPHR was banned in 1992, Fazal Ahmed was arrested, tortured, and sentenced to five years in prison, part of a broader campaign to silence Rohingya democratic representation. He remains a symbol of lawful resistance.

people.biography:
Gani Markan was one of the first elected Arakanese Indian legislators in British Burma. He was elected to the Legislative Council of Burma during the 1936 Burmese general election from the Maungdaw-Buthidaung constituency in Arakan Division. The seats in the council were divided into categories like Burmese national, Kayin, Anglo-Burman, Indian, Chinese, and European. Markan, though of Indian origin, was elected in the Burmese national category, reflecting the claim by Arakanese Indians to be a native community, distinct from other immigrants.

Among the children of E. K. Marakan, two of his sons became prominent figures in Burmese politics: his eldest son, E. G. S. Maracan (Esmail Ghani Shah Maracan), and E. D. S. Maracan (Esmail Dawood Shah Maracan). E. G. S. Maracan was widely known as Gani Maracan (Gani Markin). In 1936, Gani Maracan became a legislative representative for northern Sittwe District. He was also an enthusiastic horseman who bred horses and regularly participated in horse races, in which he also won championships. E. D. S. Maracan, Dawood Shah Maracan, was popularly known as Tanbi Saheb and was one of the leaders who worked to bring an end to the communal violence of 1942. Both brothers were awarded medals associated with King George VI, the father of Queen Elizabeth II.

people.biography:
Jafar Kawal was born in 1920 in Maungdaw Township, Arakan (now Rakhine State, Myanmar). He was a prominent Rohingya nationalist and a key figure in the Mujahid movement that emerged in the late 1940s in response to political and social injustices faced by the Rohingya community.

In 1947, Jafar Kawal founded the Mujahid Party under the Dobboro Chaung Declaration, aiming to establish an autonomous Muslim state in northern Arakan within the Union of Burma. His movement gained significant traction, with estimates of up to 2,500 fighters mobilized by 1951. The Mujahids sought to protect the rights and dignity of the Rohingya people, advocating for their recognition and autonomy.

Jafar Kawal was not only a political leader but also a poet and singer, using his artistic talents to inspire and mobilize the masses. His songs, often infused with the poetry of Allama Iqbal, resonated deeply with the Rohingya community and became anthems of resistance and unity.

In 1951, Jafar Kawal was assassinated, leading to a temporary fragmentation of the Mujahid movement. Despite his death, his legacy endured, influencing subsequent generations of Rohingya activists and leaders.

Major Faizi (Faiz) was a distinguished education officer and community leader from Maungdaw, North Arakan, active during the late British colonial period and early post-independence era. He served as the District Education Officer for Maungdaw and the Inspector of Schools for North Arakan from the 1920s until 1942. He also served as the Headmaster of the State High School in Maungdaw.

One of his most notable contributions was promoting inclusive education by appointing teachers from all communities—Rohingya, Rakhine, and Hindu—without discrimination. In recognition of his service, a ward in Maungdaw town was named Faizi Ward.

people.biography:
Master Aman Ullah is one of the most respected living historians of the Rohingya people. Born in 1950 in Maungdaw, Arakan (Rakhine State), Myanmar, he has spent over five decades documenting Rohingya history, defending their identity, and advocating for their rights through education and writing.

He began his career as a teacher after graduating from the Rangoon Teachers’ Training Institute (1969–1971) and served in various schools in Arakan for 15 years, eventually becoming a Senior Assistant Teacher. He later completed a Bachelor of Arts, a Diploma in Education, and obtained legal certification as a Higher-Grade Pleader.

In 1985, he moved to Bangladesh and became active in the Rohingya movement in exile. He served as the Secretary General of the Arakan Rohingya National Organization (ARNO) and remains involved in Rohingya political efforts as a Central Committee member of the Arakan Rohingya National Alliance (ARNA).

Beyond activism, Master Aman Ullah is best known for his historical research and writing. He has published over 100 articles on Rohingya history, law, politics, and identity, and authored key works such as:

- The Citizenship Issue of Rohingya and Myanmar’s Policy of Denationalization (2023)

- A History of the Rohingyas to 1948 (Second Edition, 2024)

He is among the first to trace Rohingya historical roots to early Muslim settlements in Arakan during the 8th century and has documented major historical events including the 1942 Rohingya massacre, colonial-era policies, and post-independence marginalization.

In exile, he was founder member and Executive Director of International School & College (ISC), Chittagong; Managing Director and Founder Principal of Full Bright International School, Chittagong and Principal of Scholar School Chittagong, and contributed to community platforms like the Rohingya Post and Rohingya Language Foundation.

Master Aman Ullah’s work is widely respected for its scholarly depth, historical accuracy, and unwavering commitment to truth. His contributions continue to shape how Rohingya history is recorded and remembered, both within the community and internationally.

people.biography:
Maulana Muhammad Hanif is a respected Rohingya scholar best known for developing the Hanifi script, the very first writing system for the Rohingya language. Born in 1952 in northern Rathedaung township, Rakhine State, Myanmar, he came from a family of religious scholars and pursued extensive Islamic and linguistic studies. He died on 10 November 2023.

In the 1980s, Hanif created the Hanifi script to accurately represent the unique sounds of the Rohingya language. This script, written from right to left with 28 characters, has become a key tool in preserving Rohingya identity and culture.

The Hanifi script is widely used today in Rohingya schools, refugee camps, and diaspora communities to teach reading and writing. Hanif’s work gave the Rohingya people a standardized way to document their language, history, and traditions.

His legacy lives on through the Hanifi script, which remains central to Rohingya cultural preservation and education.

people.summary: A Rohingya rights activist from Buthidaung Township who founded and leads the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK), lobbying governments, human rights institutions and the United Nations from exile in Britain. He has testified before the British Parliament, the U.S. Congress, the European Parliament and the UN Human Rights Council, helped submit evidence to the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice, and in 2024 became Chairperson of the Arakan Rohingya National Council (ARNC).

Facing growing discrimination and statelessness after the 1982 Citizenship Law stripped the Rohingya of citizenship, he and his family fled the country.
In exile in the UK, founded the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK) and became its president. He has published articles in outlets such as Al Jazeera, The Guardian, Anadolu Agency and Time.

Testified before the British Parliament, the U.S. Congress, the European Parliament and the UN Human Rights Council, demanding accountability for Myanmar's generals, and helped submit evidence to the ICC and the ICJ.
Became Chairperson of the Arakan Rohingya National Council (ARNC), campaigning for Rohingya recognition, repatriation and equal rights inside Myanmar.

people.biography:
Tun Khin was born in Buthidaung Township in northern Arakan (Rakhine State), Myanmar. He comes from a prominent Rohingya family—his grandfather was elected as a Member of Parliament in Myanmar’s democratic era. Facing growing discrimination and statelessness, Tun Khin and his family fled the country after the military stripped Rohingya of their citizenship under the 1982 Citizenship Law.

Living in exile in the United Kingdom, Tun Khin founded the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK (BROUK) and currently serves as its president. Under his leadership, BROUK has become one of the most visible international Rohingya advocacy organizations, actively lobbying governments, human rights institutions, and the United Nations. He frequently speaks to global media and has published articles in outlets such as Al Jazeera, The Guardian, Anadolu Agency, and Time magazine.

He has testified before the British Parliament, U.S. Congress, European Parliament, and the UN Human Rights Council, consistently demanding justice for the Rohingya people and accountability for military generals in Myanmar. He played a key role in submitting evidence to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ), supporting investigations into genocide and crimes against humanity.

Tun Khin has participated in dozens of conferences and interviews across the world, and met with key global leaders. He has also collaborated with other Rohingya leaders and diaspora groups to build stronger political unity.

In 2024, he became the Chairperson of the Arakan Rohingya National Council (ARNC), a political coalition representing Rohingya voices worldwide. Through this position, he has pushed for broader engagement with global institutions, and continues to campaign for Rohingya recognition, repatriation, and equal rights inside Myanmar.

His decades-long struggle reflects the voice of millions of Rohingya who remain stateless, silenced, and displaced. Tun Khin remains one of the most consistent and committed international advocates for Rohingya justice.

people.name: Mawlana Pir Muzzaffar Ahmad
people.birthplace: Mee Chaung Zay, Buthidaung Township, Arakan

people.summary: A Rohingya Islamic scholar, Muhaddith and spiritual guide (Pir) from Mee Chaung Zay in Buthidaung Township, who devoted his life to teaching Hadith, Fiqh and the Qur'an, to spiritual guidance and to healing. He went to India for higher studies in 1947 and returned home in 1957; in 1977 the ulama of Arakan appointed him chairman of their committee with the title Khalifatul Muslimeen. Respected by Muslims across Arakan, he was also sought out for advice and treatment by many Buddhists and people of other faiths.

timeline.text: Born on 29 October in Mee Chaung Zay, Buthidaung Township.
Studied at local Arabic and Urdu schools: the Mee Chaung Zay Arabic primary school (1934), an Urdu middle school in Hpon Nyo Leik village, and the Paung Taw Pyin Madrasa (1940).
Travelled to India in June for higher studies.

Returned home in February to serve his people and country, and devoted his life to teaching Hadith, Fiqh and the Qur'an and to spiritual purification. He became known as a clear and capable teacher, a healer of physical and spiritual suffering, and a guide to scholars and ordinary people alike.
Helped establish a religious organisation in Bangladesh to protect Islamic teachings, and served as a central council leader of what became Khuddamul Islam and later Hemayatul Islam.

people.biography:
Mawlana Pir Muzzaffar Ahmad was a renowned Rohingya Islamic scholar, Muhaddith, and spiritual guide (Pir), known for his lifelong service to the Rohingya community through religious teaching, spiritual leadership, writing, social guidance, and healing. He was deeply respected by Muslims across Arakan and also admired by many Buddhists and people of other faiths who sought his advice and treatment. He was widely regarded as a rare scholar of strong character, a defender of oppressed people, a Deobandi-trained alim, and a senior spiritual successor (khalifah) connected to the tradition of Mawlana Husain Ahmad Madani.

He was born on  29 October 1927, in Mee Chaung Zay, Buthidaung Township. He began his studies in local Arabic and Urdu schools, including Mee Chaung Zay Arabic primary school (1934), an Urdu middle school in Hpon Nyo Leik village, and Paung Taw Pyin Madrasa (1940).

In June 1947, he traveled to India for higher studies. He returned home in February 1957 to serve his people and country. His life was dedicated to teaching Hadith, Fiqh, Qur’an, and spiritual purification. He was known as a clear and capable teacher, a healer for physical and spiritual suffering, and a guide for both scholars and ordinary people. He was skilled in Urdu, English, and Arabic, and recognized as a Muhaddith and spiritual Pir.

In 1971, he helped establish a religious organization in Bangladesh aimed at protecting Islamic teachings. He served as a central council leader in what became known as Khuddamul Islam and later Hemayatul Islam. In 1977, Arakan ulama formed a committee and appointed him as chairman, also granting him the title Khalifatul Muslimeen. Through these roles, he worked for the religious and social welfare of his community.

He authored two books: Jala’ al-Qulub, a work on Sufi spiritual training based on earlier classical texts, and Ishq Ahlian Burma, which documents oppression against Arakan people and serves as a historical record for future generations.

He was also associated with unity efforts around Burma’s independence era and was said to have signed agreements connected to cooperation among communities, believing Rohingya contributions to independence were often overlooked in official history.

Mawlana Pir Muzzaffar Ahmad passed away in 2006 after a lifetime of service. He is remembered as a major Rohingya alim, spiritual guide, teacher, writer, and community leader who dedicated his life to knowledge, faith, and the welfare of his people.

people.name: Mohammed Noor
people.role: Media entrepreneur and founder of RVision
people.epithet: Giving the Rohingya a screen and a script
people.summary: A Rohingya media entrepreneur, born in Makkah to a Rohingya refugee family from Arakan, who founded Rohingya Vision (RVision), a Rohingya satellite television channel and digital news platform for the diaspora. He also established the Rohingya Football Club and led initiatives to digitise the Rohingya alphabet, create fonts and secure the Rohingya script's inclusion in the Unicode standard in 2018.

people.biography:
Mohammed Noor was born in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, to a Rohingya refugee family originally from Arakan (Rakhine State), Myanmar. Growing up stateless outside his ancestral homeland, he dedicated his life to amplifying Rohingya voices worldwide through media, technology, and advocacy.

He founded Rohingya Vision (RVision), the world’s first Rohingya satellite television channel and digital news platform. RVision serves millions in the Rohingya diaspora by providing news, education, and cultural programming from a Rohingya perspective.

Noor also established the Rohingya Football Club (RFC), a national team representing Rohingya youth internationally. RFC promotes unity, pride, and global visibility for Rohingya identity through sports.

He played a key role in developing Rohingya language technology, leading initiatives to digitize Rohingya alphabets, create fonts, and secure the Rohingya script’s inclusion in the Unicode standard in 2018. This work enables Rohingya language use across computers and smartphones, helping preserve and teach their culture.

Additionally, Noor co-founded the Rohingya Genocide Archive, which documents atrocities committed against Rohingya civilians, aiding accountability efforts worldwide.

His memoir, "Born to Struggle" (2019), shares his personal journey as a Rohingya refugee and leader of digital activism.

people.name: Mohib Ullah

Called the "Peace Father" by refugees for his calm, non-violent leadership, he addressed the UN Human Rights Council in 2019, met U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House, and campaigned for the safe return of the Rohingya with full rights. He was shot dead by unidentified gunmen in Kutupalong camp on 29 September 2021.

Addressed the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, calling for justice and safe return.

Shot and killed by unidentified gunmen in Kutupalong camp on 29 September.
timeline.note: His assassination was condemned internationally.

people.biography:
Mohib Ullah was one of the most prominent Rohingya human rights defenders of his time. Born in 1971 in Arakan, Myanmar, he spent much of his life advocating for the rights, dignity, and safe return of the Rohingya people.

He held a B.Sc. degree from Sittway University, and in 2010, became the chairman of the Buthidaung Maungdaw Regional Development Association (BMRDA). His activism expanded globally when he began documenting atrocities against Rohingya and writing about their struggle on RohingyaBlogger.com from 2012.

After the 2017 genocide, Mohib Ullah co-founded the Arakan Rohingya Society for Peace and Human Rights (ARSPH) in the Kutupalong refugee camp, Bangladesh. It quickly became one of the largest and most organized Rohingya-led civil society groups in exile. Under his leadership, ARSPH worked on education, community organizing, documentation of abuses, and advocating for repatriation with full rights.

He earned the title "Peace Father" from refugees for his calm leadership and non-violent approach. Mohib Ullah became the voice of the Rohingya in key international spaces:

- In March 2019, he addressed the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, calling for justice and safe return.

- In July 2019, he met U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House, where he directly asked what the U.S. would do to help the Rohingya return home with rights and safety.

- In August 2019, he organized a mass commemoration of the genocide anniversary with over 200,000 refugees in Kutupalong refugee camp, Bangladesh.

He rejected armed movements and always insisted that the Rohingya struggle should remain peaceful and focused on truth, rights, and justice. He also worked to unite different Rohingya voices in exile, despite facing internal and external threats.

On 29 September 2021, Mohib Ullah was shot and killed by unidentified gunmen in Kutupalong camp. His assassination was condemned internationally and marked a huge loss for the Rohingya community.

Mohib Ullah's legacy is remembered through his fearless voice, dedication to peace, and tireless defense of Rohingya identity and dignity.

people.biography:
Nay San Lwin (Zafar Shah) is a prominent Rohingya political activist and a leading voice in the global advocacy for Rohingya rights and justice. Born in 1978 in Buthidaung, Arakan (now Rakhine State, Myanmar), and raised in Rangoon (Yangon), he hails from a family with a legacy of civil service. His great-grandfather, Abdul Zolil, was officially recognized as an indigenous person in Burma.

Since leaving Myanmar, Nay San Lwin has dedicated himself to documenting human rights violations and military campaigns in Arakan State. He provides information and analysis to governments, human rights organizations, United Nations staff, and journalists to raise awareness of the Rohingya crisis.

In July 2025, Nay San Lwin was appointed Co-Chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council (ARNC), a unified political platform representing Rohingya communities from Myanmar, refugee camps in Bangladesh, and the global diaspora.

He has been publicly attacked by Myanmar's presidential office and the State Counsellor's office for his role in disseminating news about military atrocities in Northern Arakan State.

Nay San Lwin continues to be a leading voice for the Rohingya community, advocating for justice, recognition, and protection for his people.

Under his leadership ARNO has urged the UN, the OIC, ASEAN and major powers to investigate and prosecute Myanmar's military for genocide and crimes against humanity.

people.biography:
Nurul Islam is a veteran Rohingya lawyer and political activist. He was born in 1948 in Chilkhali, Maungdaw Township, Rakhine State, Myanmar. He earned a B.A. (Law) and LL.B. from the University of Rangoon in 1972–73. Later, he completed human rights training at the University of New South Wales and received an LL.M. in Human Rights from the University of East London in 2007.

He joined the Rohingya political movement in the 1960s as a student leader. He served as President of the Rangoon University Rohingya Students Association in 1971. He also co-founded and led several insurgent and nationalist groups, including the Rohingya Patriotic Front and Rohingya Solidarity Organization, eventually merging them into the Arakan Rohingya National Organisation (ARNO) in 1998, where he became its first Chairman.

Since joining ARNO, Nurul Islam has been a central figure in Rohingya advocacy. He served as consultant on Arakan affairs for the Euro-Burma Office in Brussels until 2010. He now divides his time between Chittagong, Bangladesh, and East London, UK, while leading ARNO and coordinating policy at the Free Rohingya Coalition.

Nurul Islam has been a key figure in global advocacy for Rohingya rights as chairman of the Arakan Rohingya National Organisation (ARNO). Under his leadership, ARNO urged international bodies such as the UN, OIC, ASEAN, and major powers to investigate and prosecute Myanmar’s military for genocide and crimes against humanity. In 2011, during the Rohingya Global Day of Action in London, he emphasized the community’s historical roots in Arakan and demanded the restoration of citizenship, citing their political presence since the 15th century. He continues to call for UN-led inquiries and ICC action to hold Myanmar accountable for atrocities against Rohingya civilians.

people.biography:
Qari Arshad Hussain was a Rohingya Islamic scholar, teacher, and radio broadcaster. He was born in 1910 in Oudaung Village near Maungdaw and studied Islamic sciences at Darul Uloom Deoband in India from 1939 to 1947. After returning to Myanmar, he taught at several Islamic schools, including Sufia, Lokmania, and Jamiya Forkania.

In 1961, he became the first known Rohingya to recite the Qur'an on Burma's national radio service, the Burma Broadcasting Service. He also presented news and Qur'anic recitations in the Rohingya language. The Rohingya-language program was discontinued in 1965. After fleeing Myanmar following the 2017 military campaign, he continued teaching in Balukhali Rohingya Refugee Camp in Bangladesh until his death in 2021.

people.biography:
Razia Sultana is a prominent Rohingya lawyer, researcher, and human rights activist born in Maungdaw, Rakhine State, Myanmar. She currently practices law in Bangladesh, working directly with Rohingya refugees. Her work focuses on documenting trauma, mass rape, and human trafficking suffered by Rohingya women during Myanmar’s military operations.

Since 2014, Sultana has conducted extensive field research, interviewing hundreds of survivors and documenting their testimonies in influential reports like Witness to Horror (2017) and Rape by Command (2018), which exposed the systematic use of sexual violence by Myanmar security forces during the 2016–2017 "clearance operations."

She serves as Coordinator for Women and Children’s Affairs at the Free Rohingya Coalition (FRC) and founded the Rohingya Women Welfare Society (RWWS). For her tireless activism, she was honored with the International Women of Courage Award (2019) by the U.S. Department of State, becoming the first Rohingya woman to receive the award.

people.name: Romarun
people.role: Poet and editor
