people.summary: Rohingya poet from Sittwe whose poems appeared on Rohingya Today, Arakan Pen and The Art Garden Rohingya, where she became an editor in 2020. She wrote of a life without a shore, of being left behind and of longing for the homeland, and kept up her editorial work until the end of her life. She died in 2020, at thirty-eight.
people.quote: I usually write poetry only when I feel something deeply in my heart.

timeline.text: Born Rokaiyah, also known as Ma Hla Hla Win, on 6 November in Nazi Village, Sittwe. Her parents, U Wali Ullah and Daw Sawfura, came from Myoma Ngakhura in Maungdaw Township.
Earned a B.Sc. degree specialising in Chemistry. She married at twenty-one, and later gave birth to her son, Osman.

Published poems online in Rohingya Today, Arakan Pen and The Art Garden Rohingya, among them "Kan Pyout Bawa" (A Life Without a Shore), "Shan Yit Khae Tot" (When Left Behind), "Ywet War" (The Yellow Leaf), "Pyone San Par-Mi Yoe" (Smile, Mother) and "Mway Yat Myay Tan Shin" (Longing for the Homeland).
Fell ill with lung cancer, and was treated continuously in Myanmar and abroad.
Became an editor of The Art Garden Rohingya in February, and carried the work with dedication to the end of her life. Her last poem was "Chit Thaw May May" (Beloved Mother).
Died at 4 p.m. on 17 October, aged thirty-eight.
timeline.note: In her memory, The Art Garden Rohingya published her poems as "The Last Footsteps of Romarun".

people.biography:
Poet Romarun was born on November 6, 1981, in Nazi Village, Sittwe, Arakan State. Her birth name was Rokaiyah, also known as Ma Hla Hla Win. Her parents were U Wali Ullah (also known as U Kyaw Win) and Daw Sawfura. Her parents were originally from Myoma Ngakhura, Maungdaw Township, Arakan State.

She received her basic education in Sittwe and later pursued higher education, earning a Bachelor of Science (B.Sc.) degree with a specialization in Chemistry. At the age of 21, she married and later gave birth to a son named Osman.

Romarun had a deep passion for reading and writing. In an interview, she once said, “I usually write poetry only when I feel something deeply in my heart.” She wrote and published numerous poems on online platforms such as Rohingya Today, Arakan Pen, and The Art Garden Rohingya. Among her well-known poems are Kan Pyout Bawa (A Life Without a Shore), Shan Yit Khae Tot (When Left Behind), Ywet War(The Yellow Leaf), Pyone San Par-Mi Yoe (Smile, Mother), and Mway Yat Myay Tan Shin (Longing for the Homeland).

After contributing poems to The Art Garden Rohingya, Romarun became an editor of the platform in February 2020. She carried out her editorial responsibilities with dedication and goodwill until the final period of her life. Her last poem was entitled “Chit Thaw May May” (Beloved Mother). Romarun was also particularly fond of the literary works of A Kyi Taw. Explaining why she admired his writing, she once said, “His works not only entertain readers and make them laugh, but also offer them a wide range of literary emotions and experiences.”

Romarun had been suffering from lung cancer since early 2019 and underwent continuous medical treatment both within the country and abroad. However, death spares no one. Whether young or old, wise or strong, when one’s appointed time comes, departure from this world is inevitable. Every living soul must surely taste death. At 4:00 p.m. on October 17, 2020, Romarun bade farewell to her beloved mother and her only son and returned to Allah in accordance with His divine will.

Following Romarun’s death, The Art Garden Rohingya published a collection of her poems entitled The Last Footsteps of Romarun in her memory.

people.biography:
Selim Noor is a Rohingya humanitarian and media figure based in Istanbul, known for his work in raising awareness about the Rohingya crisis and strengthening Rohingya identity through media, education, and community initiatives.

Originally connected to Mecca, Saudi Arabia, and now living in Istanbul, Turkey, he is active in Rohingya civil society and diaspora efforts. He is fluent in formal Arabic, which has allowed him to engage with Arabic-speaking audiences and media on Rohingya issues.

He is a co-founder of Arakan News Agency (ANA), a Rohingya-focused news platform that reports on Rohingya affairs and the situation in Arakan. He is also a co-founder of the Arakan Humanitarian Association in Turkey, which works on humanitarian support, awareness, and youth engagement for Rohingya communities.

people.name: Shamsul Anwarul Huq
people.role: Academic, former politician and pro-democracy activist
people.epithet: From the classroom to the struggle for democracy
people.summary: Shamsul Anwarul Huq, also known as Kyaw Min, is a Rohingya academic, educator and pro-democracy activist from Buthidaung, Arakan. A former teacher and primary school headmaster, he became a leading figure in the National Democratic Party for Human Rights (NDPHR) and was elected Member of Parliament for Buthidaung-1 in the 1990 general election, but the military junta banned the party and prevented him from taking his seat. In 1998 Aung San Suu Kyi invited him to join the Committee Representing the People's Parliament (CRPP). In 2005 he was arrested and sentenced to 47 years in prison, and the imprisonment of his family with him, including his daughters Wai Wai Nu and Khin Khin Nu, drew international attention to the persecution of Rohingya political figures.

timeline.note: The military junta banned the NDPHR and prevented him from taking his seat, but he continued to campaign for citizenship rights and equality.

people.biography:
Shamsul Anwarul Huq, also known as Kyaw Min, is a distinguished Rohingya academic, educator, and pro-democracy activist born in Buthidaung, Arakan. After graduating in Economics and obtaining a Diploma in Educational Practice from institutions in Rangoon, he began his career in 1969 with the Myanmar Education Department. His early, significant work for the Rohingya community focused on promoting education and literacy, serving as a teacher and primary school headmaster in Arakan.

Huq’s activism intensified during the 1988 pro-democracy movement, leading to his political career and dismissal from the education sector. He became a crucial figure in the National Democratic Party for Human Rights (NDPHR) and was overwhelmingly elected as a Member of Parliament for the Buthidaung-1 constituency in the 1990 general election. Although the military junta banned the NDPHR and prevented him from taking his seat, he continued to campaign for citizenship rights and equality. His importance to the national pro-democracy struggle was further cemented when Aung San Suu Kyi invited him to join the Committee Representing the People’s Parliament (CRPP) in 1998.

His decades of peaceful resistance were met with severe persecution. Huq was repeatedly detained in 1992 and 1994, and most dramatically in 2005, when he was arrested and unjustly sentenced to 47 years in prison under discriminatory laws. His imprisonment, alongside that of his wife and children (including his daughters Wai Wai Nu and Khin Khin Nu), drew significant international attention to the systematic persecution of Rohingya political figures.

people.biography:
Shaykh Abdul Wali al‑Arkani, also called Abu Muʿāḍ, was born in 1983 in Mislafah, Mecca, to a Rohingya-origin family from Arakan (Rakhine State, Myanmar). He memorized the Quran early, guided by his father and other teachers, beginning formal recitation studies at age 14, particularly under notable scholars including Shaykh Harun Dahir, the late Shaykh Muhammad Kabir, and Shaykh Muhammad Idriss Abbass.

He joined the Al-Arqam Ibn Abu Al-Arqam Institute at Masjid al‑Haram and graduated in 1997. His first imamate role was at age 13 in Mecca at the mosque of Shaykh Muhammad Saleh Jamal. After serving in various Mecca mosques, he became Imam of Khādim al-Haramayn ash-Sharifayn in Jeddah, preaching and reciting Taraweeh and regular prayers.

He has been officially invited to lead prayers alongside esteemed reciters such as Mishary Rashid al-Afasy in Ajman, UAE, an honor reflecting his rising reputation. His distinctive, melodious Quran recitations are recorded and broadcast across major Arab channels in Saudi Arabia, Abu Dhabi, and Bahrain, and are available on platforms like Assabile.com and Quran Central.

people.biography:
Sheikh Abdul Majeed al-Arakani (الشيخ عبد المجيد الأركاني) is a renowned Rohingya Qari and Quran reciter born in Saudi Arabia to a Rohingya refugee family originally from Arakan (Rakhine State), Myanmar. Growing up in Saudi Arabia, he memorized the Holy Quran at an early age under the guidance of prominent Quranic scholars and mastered the rules of Tajweed and Qira'at.

He gained wide recognition across the Islamic world for his soulful, melodious, and emotionally resonant Quranic recitations. Sheikh Abdul Majeed has served as an Imam leading daily and Taraweeh prayers at prominent mosques in Saudi Arabia. His recitations are widely broadcast on Islamic television channels, radio stations, and online Quranic platforms (such as Assabile, Quran Central, and Islamway), serving as a distinguished cultural and spiritual representative for the Rohingya diaspora worldwide.

people.role: Qari and Imam of the Prophet's Mosque

people.summary: A Rohingya Qari and scholar of the Quran who, in 1990, was appointed Imam of the Prophet's Mosque (Al-Masjid an-Nabawi) in Medina, a historic achievement for a Rohingya. Born in Mecca in 1952 to a family of Rohingya refugees who had fled persecution in Arakan, he grew up in hardship, memorized the Quran by the age of 13, and earned master's and doctorate degrees in Tafsir and Quranic sciences at the Islamic University of Madinah, where he later joined the faculty. He was known for his emotional, clear and deeply spiritual recitation.

people.biography:
Muhammad Ayyub was a renowned Rohingya Islamic scholar, Qari, and Imam, best known for his powerful recitation of the Quran and his service as an Imam of Al-Masjid an-Nabawi in Medina. He was one of the most respected Rohingya figures in the Islamic world.

He was born in October 1952 in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, to a family of Rohingya refugees who had fled persecution in Arakan (Rakhine State), Burma. His early life was marked by hardship and poverty. Despite this, he memorized the Quran by age 13 under the guidance of Sheikh Khalil Al-Qari.

He pursued higher Islamic studies in Medina, earning a bachelor's degree in Sharia, followed by master’s and doctorate degrees in Tafsir and Quranic sciences from the Islamic University of Madinah, where he later became a faculty member.

In 1990 (1410 AH), Sheikh Ayyub was appointed Imam of the Prophet’s Mosque, a historic achievement for a Rohingya. He held the position until 1997, then served as Imam of Quba Mosque until his final years. In Ramadan 2015, he was again appointed to lead Taraweeh prayers at Al-Masjid an-Nabawi, a moment of honor for Rohingya Muslims worldwide.

He was known for his emotional, clear, and deeply spiritual recitation, widely listened to and loved across the Muslim world. He followed the Hanafi school of thought and was deeply connected to classical Islamic scholarship.

Sheikh Muhammad Ayyub passed away on 16 April 2016 in Medina. His funeral prayer was held in the Prophet’s Mosque, and he was buried in Al-Baqi Cemetery.

He is remembered not only as a great Qari and scholar, but as a proud Rohingya who reached the highest levels of Islamic leadership through knowledge, perseverance, and sincerity.

people.biography:
Shobu, officially named Shobbir Ahmed, was a legendary Rohingya singer and performer. Born around 1950 in Myoma Khayandan, Maungdaw, (Arakan)  Rakhine State, he became a household name across Rohingya communities for his emotional and patriotic songs. He is remembered as one of the greatest cultural figures in Rohingya history.

In the 1970s and 1980s, Shobu became the lead singer of the Arakanese Rohingya theatre in Maungdaw and Buthidaung. He used his voice to speak about the suffering, love, and hopes of the Rohingya people. His performances often combined music and drama, playing a major role in shaping Rohingya cultural identity.

His most famous songs, like “Arakanor Meri Herejohar,” moved listeners to tears and reminded them of their deep connection to their homeland. His songs were not just entertainment — they were emotional, historical, and political expressions of a people in crisis.

In 1980, due to rising persecution in Burma, Shobu migrated to Saudi Arabia. Even in exile, he continued singing and remained an active voice for his people. His songs became a source of comfort and pride for the Rohingya diaspora, helping preserve their language, history, and spirit.

Shobu died on 19 November 2009 in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, after a long struggle with kidney disease. He was buried there the following day. His passing was deeply mourned across Rohingya communities worldwide.

people.summary: A Bengali poet of the royal court of Arakan's Mrauk U kingdom, born in 1607 in Jalalpur, Bengal, and brought to Arakan in his youth after Portuguese pirates captured him. With the patronage of the prime minister Magan Thakur and the royal minister Syed Musa he wrote Padmavati (1648), a Bengali adaptation of Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Hindi epic, completed Daulat Qazi's unfinished Satimayna O Lorchandrani, and rendered Persian works of Nizami into Bengali, earning the title Pandit Kabi (Wise Poet).

timeline.text: Born in Jalalpur, Fatehabad Pargana, into an aristocratic family; his father was a minister under the ruler of Fatehabad. He mastered Bengali, Arabic, Persian and Sanskrit, and was trained in music and warfare.
Captured by Portuguese pirates while travelling with his father, and taken to Arakan.

First served as a bodyguard; his poetic talent later won him a place at the royal court of King Sanda Thudhamma, with the patronage of the prime minister Magan Thakur and the royal minister Syed Musa.

people.biography:
Syed Alaol was born in 1607 in Jalalpur, Fatehabad Pargana, Bengal Subah (now part of Madaripur District, Bangladesh). He hailed from an aristocratic family; his father served as a minister under the ruler of Fatehabad. Alaol was well-educated, mastering Bengali, Arabic, Persian, and Sanskrit, and was also trained in music and warfare .

In his youth, Alaol was captured by Portuguese pirates while traveling with his father and was taken to Arakan (Rakhine State, Myanmar). Initially serving as a bodyguard, he later gained recognition for his poetic talents and was appointed to the royal court of King Sanda Thudhamma of the Mrauk U dynasty. There, he received patronage from prominent figures such as Magan Thakur, the prime minister, and Syed Musa, the royal minister .

Alaol's literary contributions are significant. His most famous work, "Padmavati" (1648), is a Bengali adaptation of Malik Muhammad Jayasi's Hindi epic, blending Sufi themes with local folklore. Other notable works include:

- "Satimayna O Lorchandrani" (1659): Completed from Daulat Qazi's unfinished manuscript.

- "Saptapaykar" (1665): A Bengali rendition of Nizami Ganjavi's Persian text.

- "Saifulmuluk Badiuzzamal" (1669): A love story between a prince and a fairy.

- "Sikandarnama" (1671–72): A translation of Nizami's "Eskander-nama" .

Alaol's works are celebrated for their lyrical beauty and intellectual depth, earning him the title "Pandit Kabi" (Wise Poet). His legacy is honored in Bangladesh through the Alaol Sahitya Puroshkar, a literary award named in his honor .

people.name: Tekkatho Nanda Meik
people.role: Writer, novelist and editor
people.epithet: The man who asked for heaven and earth
people.summary: Writer, novelist, poet, editor and publisher from Taungup, remembered as "the man who asked for heaven and earth". He edited Myawaddy Magazine and other leading journals, wrote dozens of books, many of them novels, translated works of war and military history, and produced one of Burma's earliest translated works of wartime memoir literature.

timeline.text: Born Mohammed Ali, also called Maung Tin Aung, on 8 March in Taungup, Thandwe District — the elder of twins. His father, U Maung Maung Gyi, was a township official in Taungup.
During the Japanese occupation, took part in anti-fascist student movements alongside the lecturer U Kyaw Yin, later Rector of Mandalay University.
Passed the matriculation examination at the Government Anglo-Burmese High School in Thandwe, with distinction in English, and went on to Rangoon University.
His earliest known work, the poem "Maung Do Rakhine Pyi" (Our Arakan), appeared in the December issue of Journal Kyaw.

Associate editor of the Burmese section of the Rangoon University Annual Magazine and editor of the Arakanese and Burmese Muslim students' magazines; won first prize in a short-story competition with "Kabyar Ta Kyawt".
Left university and published his first full-length novel, "Nandar Pearl"; became an assistant editor at the Toe Tat Yay (Progress) newspaper.
High-school teacher at the Government High School in Wakema.
Editor of Yaung Chi Journal and, from the same year, managing editor and editor-in-chief of Myawaddy Magazine; published the novels "Maung Gyi Lar Par Hay" and "Pan Taing Hmwe Par Say".

Edited Yoke Shin Padetha and Nawaday magazines, started Detective Magazine with the writer Moe Wai, and wrote a stream of novels, among them "Thway Thitsar" (Blood Oath), along with the guide "Sar Yay Chin Thaw Thu Myar Tho" (To Those Who Want to Write).

Published full-length translations of war and military history, among them "The Battle of Imphal", "Burma: The Battlefield" and "Thanlwin Myit Kan Taik Pwe" (The Battle on the Banks of the Thanlwin River).
Published a further run of full-length books, among them "Saipan Kyun Taik Pwe" (The Battle of Saipan) and "Myitkyina Taik Pwe" (The Battle of Myitkyina).
Kept publishing to the end of his life, including two-volume translations of "Titanic" and "Thway Set Chay Yar" (Trail of Blood).
Died at 10:05 p.m. on Saturday, 15 November, at House No. 991, Aung Mingalar Lane, Ywama East, Insein.
timeline.note: His twin, Tekkatho Zaw Min, founded the Twin Brothers publishing house in his memory. In 2004 his former students published "Tekkatho Nanda Meik, or The Man Who Asked for Heaven and Earth".

people.biography:
Tekkatho Nanda Meik, who was figuratively described as “one who asked for heaven and earth,” was a prominent Muslim figure from Arakan. He was renowned as a writer, novelist, poet, editor, and literary publisher, as well as the author of one of Burma’s earliest translated works of wartime memoir literature.

Tekkatho Nanda Meik was born on Thursday, March 8, 1923, during the colonial period, in Taungup, Thandwe District. He was the son of U Maung Maung Gyi, a township official in Taungup, and Daw Shwe. He had three siblings: Maung Tin Aung, Maung Tin Maung, and Ma Tin Tin. He was the elder of a pair of twins. His birth name was Mohammed Ali, also known as Maung Tin Aung, while his parents affectionately called him “Ko Ko.”

Mohammed Ali received his early education at the National Burmese Middle School in Taungup, where he studied up to the fifth standard. After moving with his family to Thandwe, he passed the matriculation examination in 1946 from the Government Anglo-Burmese High School in Thandwe, earning a distinction in English. He subsequently continued his education at Rangoon University. While serving as an executive member of the Thandwe Students’ Union, he participated alongside lecturer U Kyaw Yin in anti-fascist student movements during the Japanese occupation.

Nanda Meik entered the literary world with his poem “Maung Do Rakhine Pyi” (Our Arakan), published in the December 1947 issue of Journal Kyaw (Vol. 11, No. 3). The poem is believed to be his earliest known literary work.

In 1949–50, Nanda Meik served as associate editor of the Burmese-language section of the Rangoon University Annual Magazine. He also served as editor of the magazine of the Rangoon University Arakanese Students’ Association and as editor of the magazine of the Rangoon University Burmese Muslim Students’ Association. In addition, he held the position of Vice-President of the Rangoon University Arakanese Students’ Association. In a short-story competition organized by the Rangoon University Arakanese Association, he won first prize for his short story “Kabyar Ta Kyawt”, which he submitted under the name “Maung Tin Aung (B.A. Senior)”. During the same year, his play “Ko Pyauk Say Lone” (The Invisibility Pill) was published in the Rangoon University Annual Magazine (Vol. 1, No. 3). His poem “Khit-e-Kyemon” (Mirror of the Age), described as a tay gyo (lyrical prelude), was also published in Taw Win Magazine and in the magazine of the Arakanese Students’ Association.

In 1950, Nanda Meik left university without sitting for his final B.A. examination. That year, he wrote and published his first full-length novel, “Nandar Pearl”. During the Japanese occupation, he had also participated in anti-Japanese resistance activities alongside U Kyaw Yin, who later became Rector of Mandalay University. After leaving university, Nanda Meik worked as an assistant editor at the Toe Tat Yay (Progress) newspaper. In 1953, he became a high school teacher at the Government High School in Wakema.

In 1954, Nanda Meik became editor of Yaung Chi Journal, published by Myawaddy Magazine. In the same year, he also took on the roles of managing editor and editor-in-chief of Myawaddy Magazine, positions he held until 1960. During this period, he published the full-length novel Maung Gyi Lar Par Hay (Maung Gyi, Come Here). In 1956, he wrote and published the novel Pan Taing Hmwe Par Say (May Every Flower Be Fragrant). In 1960, he served as editor of Yoke Shin Padetha Magazine and as editor-in-chief of Nawaday Magazine. Together with the writer Moe Wai, he also took the lead in publishing Detective Magazine, serving as its editor. He also wrote and published Shwe Pyi Gyi, a novel set against the background of Burmese history, and Pan Phwet Tan,a romantic novel based on traditional Arakanese customs and culture.

In 1961, Nanda Meik published several original novels, including Thway Thitsar (Blood Oath), Saw Kyo Hlae Par, Chit Thaw Ni Ni (Beloved Ni Ni), Achit Lan Kalay Winga Bar (The Labyrinth of Love), Moe Tein Ko Hmyaw (Looking Toward the Clouds), and Moe Tein Ko Hmar. He also compiled a collection of literary essays and published a book on writing entitled Sar Yay Chin Thaw Thu Myar Tho (To Those Who Want to Write). In 1963, he published the war novel Sit Kyaung Chi Thaw.

In 1964, Nanda Meik published the books Chindwin Kyaw Hlyin (When We Cross the Chindwin), Thway Ko Lan Khin Ywe (Paving the Road with Blood), and Thin Kyar Pay Par Lay Oo Saya (Please Continue to Teach Us, Teacher). In 1965, he wrote and published a number of full-length translated works on war and military history, including The Anti-Japanese Resistance, Life as Fragile as a Leaf, The Battle of Imphal, Kalein Seit Ngyan Sin, Burma: The Battlefield, and Through Mandalay: The Stages of Battle.

In 1966, Nanda Meik published several full-length translated works, including Thway Chaung Si Taik Pwe (The Battle of Flowing Blood), Thanlwin Myit Kan Taik Pwe (The Battle on the Banks of the Thanlwin River), Let Ta Kan Taik Pwe (Close-Quarters Battle), Ta Ti Ya Mee Kyi (The Third Firebomb), Sit Pyay (War Refugee), Sin Yal, Sanit Yal, Lu Thar Yal, and Zet Tat Phwe. In 1967, he published a number of full-length books, including Ah-Thay Khan Tat Su (The Suicide Unit), Saipan Kyun Taik Pwe (The Battle of Saipan), Htaung Ko Yar Lay Se Hnit (1942), Pan War Sit Kyaung (The Pan Wa Column), Myawaddy Sit Kyaung (The Myawaddy Column), Myitkyina Taik Pwe (The Battle of Myitkyina), Meinma Thutethana (Women: A Study), Volumes 1 and 2, and Yone Kyi Chet Atwet Athak Sunt Thu Myar (Those Who Sacrificed Their Lives for Their Beliefs). In 1968, he published such books as Bandula Khan Tat (Bandula Fort), Saw Nanda, and Moe Tein Ko Say. In 1969, he published the full-length translated works Theikpan Sone Htauk (The Science Detective) and Thone Yaung Chae Tase Thinbaw (The Three-Colored Ghost Ship). In 1971, he published Bawa Thitsar Myitta Hlaing (Waves of Life, Loyalty, and Love) and Ta Theint Theint Done. In 1977, he published the novels Se Pyi Htaung Chawt Tot Ma Pyone and Taung Ta Kar Taw, San Kaw Ne Kyar Htaung.

In 1981, Nanda Meik published Following Thay Min Nauk Tho Chay Yar Kauk Thaw (the Footsteps of Death), a two-volume work.

In 1982, he published the translated works Titanic (two volumes) and Thway Set Chay Yar (Trail of Blood), also in two volumes. In 1983, he published Ta Thaung Hmar Ta Yauk (One in Ten Thousand) and Than Khaung Yan Khunit Mee Nit (Seven Minutes Past Midnight). In 1984, he published several books, including Maha Khayee Shay (The Great Long Journey), Moe Pyo Ma Pyo, A-Twe Sein Sein, and Hitler’s Amwe (Hitler’s Legacy).

In 1985, he published Typhoon (Taik Fun), Naung Udan Be Ma Kyei Sayar, and the two-volume Bilu Si, Lu Si. In 1986, he wrote and published several full-length translated works, including Thanmani Thitsar (Steel Loyalty”) and 34-Ashay (34-East).

Tekkatho Nanda Meik remained devoted to his literary work without interruption until the final days of his life. At the age of 64, he passed away at 10:05 p.m. on Saturday, November 15, 1986, at House No. 991, Aung Mingalar Lane, Ywama East, Insein. At the time of his death, he was survived by his wife, Daw Than Nu; his daughters, Saw Thida Nanda Meik and Saw Sanda Nanda Meik; and his sons, Zeya Nanda Meik, Seinda Nanda Meik, and Okka Nanda Meik. Following his death, his twin brother, Tekkatho Zaw Min, took the lead in establishing the “Twin Brothers” Publishing House (Ahmwar Nyi Naung) in his memory. In addition, some of Nanda Meik’s former students took the initiative to compile and publish a commemorative book entitled Tekkatho Nanda Meik, or The Man Who Asked for Heaven and Earth in 2004.

people.name: U Abdul Gaffar
people.role: Member of the Constituent Assembly and politician
people.epithet: An early champion of Rohingya recognition
people.summary: A Rohingya politician and educator from Buthidaung, Arakan, remembered for his 1948 Memorandum of Appeal, which sought official recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group with their own culture, language, history and civilization. Elected to the Burmese Constituent Assembly for Buthidaung in 1947, he later sat in the Chamber of Nationalities and served as Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministry of Health under Prime Minister U Nu.

timeline.text: Born in Rwanyno Taung village, the son of Ulah Meah.
After the Chittagong Senior Madrasa, earned a B.A. from the University of Dacca (1930) and a Bachelor of Education from Aligarh Muslim University in India (1933).

people.biography:
U Abdul Gaffar was a prominent Rohingya politician and educator from Buthidaung, Arakan (Rakhine State, Myanmar). Born in 1910 in Rwanyno Taung village, he was the son of Ulah Meah. He completed his education at Chittagong Senior Madrasa, then earned a B.A. from the University of Dacca (1930) and a Bachelor of Education from Aligarh Muslim University (1933) in India. Before entering politics, he served as District Inspector of Schools in Akyab (1931–1942) and Township Officer in Buthidaung (1944–1945).

Gaffar was elected to the Burmese Constituent Assembly in 1947, representing Buthidaung, and took his oath in January 1948 after Burma’s independence. In 1949, he was appointed by President Sao Shwe Thaik to the Inquiry Commission of Arakan, which examined regional autonomy issues. He was later elected to the Chamber of Nationalities (Upper House) in 1952 from Akyab West and in 1956 from Maungdaw. He also served as Parliamentary Secretary for the Ministry of Health under Prime Minister U Nu.

Gaffar is particularly remembered for presenting a Memorandum of Appeal in 1948, seeking official recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group in Arakan. In this document, he argued that the Rohingya were a nation with a unique culture, language, history, and civilization, deserving constitutional recognition. His advocacy laid the foundation for Rohingya political identity, even though subsequent events—such as the 1962 military coup and the 1982 nationality law—later marginalized the community.

U Abdul Gaffar passed away in 1966, leaving a legacy as one of the earliest Rohingya leaders to champion constitutional recognition, minority rights, and political participation in Burma.

people.biography:
U Ba Sein is a Rohingya writer and community figure known for documenting and sharing information about the Rohingya crisis. He is best recognized as the founder of Rohingya Blogger, one of the early online platforms used to report on human rights abuses and the situation of Rohingya in Arakan (Rakhine State).

U Ba Sein worked as a civil servant in Myanmar’s Ministry of Co-operatives before later fleeing the country due to increasing discrimination and persecution against Rohingya.

In exile in the United Kingdom, he became active in advocacy and information work focused on Rohingya rights.

He has provided first-hand testimony about historical military operations against Rohingya, including the 1978 Naga Min (King Dragon) operation. His accounts have been cited in academic and policy discussions on Rohingya persecution and have helped researchers, journalists, and human rights groups understand patterns of abuse in Rakhine State.

In 2005, he founded the Rohingya Blogger website, which became a source of news, statements, and documentation related to the Rohingya community. Through writing and information-sharing, he contributed to raising international awareness about the Rohingya situation.

people.name: U Kyaw Hla Aung
people.role: Lawyer and civil rights activist
people.epithet: A steadfast defender of Rohingya rights
people.summary: U Kyaw Hla Aung, born Muhammad Kasim in Sittwe, was a Rohingya lawyer and civil rights defender who was arrested multiple times and spent years in prison under Myanmar's military regime. After qualifying as a lawyer in 1982 he defended Rohingya farmers and landowners, co-founded the National Democratic Party for Human Rights, and later worked to improve access to healthcare and education for Rohingya in the camps, becoming a respected leader in the Thet Kae Pyin internment camp near Sittwe. In 2018 he became the first Rohingya to win the Aurora Prize for Awakening Humanity.

Worked as a court clerk and stenographer.
Graduated as a lawyer, and began using his legal knowledge to defend vulnerable farmers and landowners.
Represented Rohingya farmers resisting land confiscation by the government.

people.biography:
U Kyaw Hla Aung was a pioneering Rohingya lawyer and civil rights defender, widely recognized as one of the most courageous advocates for Rohingya rights. Born as Muhammad Kasim on 16 August 1940 in Sittwe (Akyab), Rakhine State, Myanmar, he witnessed early on the systemic injustice faced by his community.

After working as a court clerk and stenographer, he trained as a lawyer and graduated in 1982. Motivated by the ongoing discrimination against Rohingya, he used his legal knowledge to defend vulnerable farmers and landowners. In 1986, he represented Rohingya farmers resisting land confiscation by the government — a courageous act that led to his first imprisonment.

Despite multiple arrests and spending years in prison under Myanmar’s military regime, U Kyaw Hla Aung remained steadfast. He co-founded the National Democratic Party for Human Rights and was a candidate in the 1990 elections, though the government blocked his political participation by arresting him and sentencing him to 14 years in prison.

He continued his activism from inside prison and later in refugee camps, where he worked tirelessly to improve access to healthcare and education for the Rohingya. He became a respected leader in the Thet Kae Pyin internment camp near Sittwe.

In 2018, U Kyaw Hla Aung became the first Rohingya — and one of the very few people from Myanmar — to win the Aurora Prize for Awakening Humanity, an international humanitarian award recognizing his extraordinary courage and dedication.

In 2019, Fortune magazine ranked him 28th in its list of the World's Greatest Leaders, and the Armenian post office honored him with a commemorative stamp.

U Kyaw Hla Aung passed away on 31 July 2021 in Yangon, Myanmar, after years of service to his people.

people.name: U Mya Than
people.role: Health officer
people.epithet: The forgotten ray
people.summary: A Rohingya health worker and leprosy specialist who served hospitals and rural health centres across Arakan for three decades, and an unsung builder of his community: he helped turn a village hut into a health centre, pressed for Taung Pyo Let Wai's clinic to become a hospital, and in retirement taught and treated people in the villages around Bawli Bazaar and organised water supplies for mosques.
people.quote: Ashá táilé rasta neele. Where there is a will, there is a way.

timeline.text: Born Delwar Ahmad in Bawli Bazaar, Maungdaw, the fourth of six brothers. His father, Qazi Bokhtar Mahmud, was a medical officer in the British Army and a Qazi; his mother was a well-known practitioner of traditional medicine.
After Maungdaw High School he trained at the Health Assistant Training School in Rangoon, and began his career as a laboratory technician at Maungdaw Hospital.
Grade I Laboratory Supervisor at Buthidaung General Hospital.

Supervisor in the leprosy departments of Sittwe General Hospital and then Buthidaung Township Hospital — a specialist so valued that hospitals kept inviting him to lecture on leprosy after he retired.
Health Officer at Thabeik Taung Rural Health Centre, where he rallied the villagers to turn a clinic that was little more than a hut into a permanent health facility.

At Taung Pyo Let Wai, he made the case to General Khin Nyunt that the health centre was too small for its patients; it was upgraded and rebuilt as a station hospital. That year he also served on the medical team of the refugee repatriation programme.

Retired to Bawli Bazaar, where he taught children who could not afford school, gave free treatment and first-aid training, and started "Water Supply for All" to bring water to mosques and other religious buildings.
Died on the morning of Thursday, 12 February — he had been born on a Thursday too — and was laid to rest at the Bawli Cemetery in Kyaik Chaung, Laung Don.

people.biography:
> “Ashá táilé rasta neele”

This was one of the sayings that Health Officer U Mya Than often used when offering advice and encouragement. He frequently quoted the original English proverb, “Where there is a will, there is a way.” It was one of his favorite sayings.

The name U Mya Than may be unfamiliar to many readers. Although he was not a nationally renowned figure, he was an unsung individual who devoted himself to serving his country and his people. As a healthcare worker, he carried out his duties faithfully, conscientiously, and with genuine dedication to the well-being of those he served.

Maung Mya Than was born in 1935 in Bawli Bazaar, Maungdaw, Arakan State, to Qazi Bokhtar Mahmud and Daw Amina Chowdhury. His birth name was Delwar Ahmad. His father served as a medical officer in the British Army and as a local medical officer in the Bawli area. He was also a Qazi appointed by the British administration with judicial authority. His mother was a well-known practitioner of traditional medicine and came from the Bawli family lineage. Mya Than was the fourth of six brothers. When he was around thirteen years old, his father, Qazi Bokhtar Mahmud, passed away. Thereafter, Mya Than grew up under the care and guidance of his mother and elder brother.

Maung Mya Than studied up to the sixth standard at the Amir Ali Urdu School of that period. When the school was later converted into a Burmese-English National School, he continued his education there. He subsequently completed his secondary education at Maungdaw High School. He had initially been interested in joining the Burmese Army, but circumstances prevented him from doing so. Influenced by his family background, he instead developed an interest in medicine and pursued medical training at the Health Assistant Training School at Aung San Stadium in Rangoon (Institute of Community Health, which was later relocated and expanded in Magway).

Maung Mya Than began his career as a laboratory technician at Maungdaw Hospital. In 1964, he was appointed Grade I Laboratory Supervisor at Buthidaung General Hospital, where he served until 1974. From 1974 to 1981, he served as a Grade II Supervisor in the Leprosy Department of Sittwe General Hospital. From 1981 to 1985, he worked as a supervisor in the Leprosy Department at Buthidaung Township Hospital. From 1985 to 1990, he served as a Health Officer at Thabeik Taung Rural Health Centre, and from 1990 to 1995, he served in the same capacity at Taung Pyo Health Centre. In 1995, he retired from government service. He spent the remaining years of his life peacefully in his native Bawli Bazaar.

During his retirement, in addition to providing medical care, U Mya Than volunteered as a teacher in the villages of Kyein Chaung, Laung Don, and Done Paik. He actively taught children who were unable to attend school because their families lacked the financial means to support their education. He also provided financial assistance, whenever possible, to students from disadvantaged families. He regularly conducted basic health education and first-aid training for people living in rural communities. He also provided free medical treatment to a remarkable number of people, setting an admirable example of service to the community. In addition, he took a particular interest in improving access to water at mosques and other religious buildings, organizing initiatives to ensure an adequate water supply. He called this initiative “Water Supply for All.”

During his years of service, Health Officer U Mya Than undoubtedly helped save many lives through health education and medical treatment. In addition, some of his lasting contributions to the country and the public, which continue to benefit local communities to this day, include the following:

(a)  When U Mya Than was assigned to Thabeik Taung, the rural health center in the Rakhine village of Thabeik Taung was little more than a small hut. During his period of service there, through his tireless efforts day and night, he mobilized the collective support of the villagers and helped transform the small clinic into a more substantial and permanent healthcare facility. To this day, the villagers remember him for his contribution.

(b)  Health Officer U Mya Than also made significant efforts toward upgrading the Taung Pyo Let Wai Health Centre into a larger hospital. During General Khin Nyunt’s visit to Taung Pyo Let Wai in 1993, U Mya Than met with him and explained that the existing health centre was inadequate for the number of patients in the area. He proposed that the facility be upgraded to a hospital. When asked about what would be required for such an expansion, he also discussed the needs and requirements for enlarging and developing the facility. Following General Khin Nyunt’s visit, the health centre was upgraded to a station hospital, and the facility itself was expanded and reconstructed. The station hospital that stands in Taung Pyo Let Wai today was therefore, according to this account, an outcome of Health Officer U Mya Than’s persistent efforts. At the time, Myanma Alinn and Kyemon newspapers reportedly covered General Khin Nyunt’s visit and published accounts of their meeting and discussions.

(c)  During the 1993 refugee repatriation programme, Health Officer U Mya Than was selected to serve as a member of the medical team. In this capacity, he actively assisted refugees returning to their original homes.

(d)  U Mya Than was a Rohingya healthcare professional with specialized expertise in leprosy. Because of his knowledge and experience in this field, he was specially transferred from Buthidaung Township Hospital to Sittwe General Hospital. Even after his retirement, he was frequently invited by the relevant hospitals to deliver health-education lectures on leprosy.

Throughout his professional career, U Mya Than devoted himself wholeheartedly to serving the public without distinction of ethnicity or religion. Even in retirement, he continued working for the welfare of his community and the wider public.

In 1961, Maung Mya Than married Daw Ma Nu, also known as Husson Jahan, the niece of Township Officer Furuk Ahmad and the third daughter of Saya Gyi Muhammad Hassan. She was descended from the Bawli and Qazi families. The couple had nine children—four daughters, Thein Thein Nu, Than Than Nu, Thein Nu, and Than Than Htwe; and five sons, Than Myint, Thein Hteik, Than Hteik, Than Tun, and Aye Tun.

Health Officer U Mya Than, who held Registration No. AK-155594, also came from a family whose members served their country and community in various capacities. His eldest brother, U Bedar Ahmad, served as a military medical officer appointed under the British administration. U Nesar Ahmad served as secretary of a village administrative body; U Maung Nu served as a high school headmaster; and his younger brother, U Mya Sein, served as a state malaria-control officer. Each contributed to public service in his respective field. His youngest brother, U Mahmud, unfortunately passed away while studying at Kyaukphyu Education College. His only sister, Daw Naw Fiza, remains alive to this day.

Health Officer U Mya Than was a man who lived a simple and modest life. He was particularly fond of children. It is said that whenever he returned from somewhere, he would almost always bring snacks in his hands for the children in his neighborhood. Whenever he went for a walk through the village, children would often gather around him. To them, the sight of “Doctor Nana” immediately brought to mind the treats he would give them. He had a great passion for reading and keeping a diary. He was proficient in both reading and writing Urdu and Bengali. He was also interested in architecture and craftsmanship. During his spare time, he enjoyed working at home with wood and cement, making chairs, tables, shelves, and other pieces in a variety of creative designs. One particularly remarkable characteristic was that, although he was naturally left-handed, he could write skillfully with either hand. As for sports, he was especially fond of playing badminton.

On the morning of Thursday, February 12, 2009, Health Officer U Mya Than bade farewell to his beloved children and returned to Allah. He had been born on a Thursday, and it was also on a Thursday that he passed away. His remains were laid to rest at the Bawli Cemetery in Kyaik Chaung, Laung Don. May Almighty Allah grant him the highest and most honored place in the Hereafter. Ameen.

people.name: U Shwe Maung
people.role: Former Member of Parliament for Buthidaung and rights activist
people.epithet: Elected in 2010, barred in 2015
people.summary: U Shwe Maung, also known as Abdul Razak, is a Rohingya politician and rights activist from Buthidaung, Arakan, who won a seat in Myanmar's House of Representatives (Pyithu Hluttaw) in the 2010 general election. During his 2011–2016 term he used his position to advocate for Rohingya rights and reconciliation in Rakhine State, but ahead of the 2015 election the Union Election Commission barred him from running, citing alleged citizenship issues concerning his parents. He later became a board member of ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights and President of the Arakan Institute for Peace and Human Rights (AiPAH).

timeline.text: Born on 30 June in Buthidaung to Rohingya Muslim parents, Abdul Hadi and Aye Sein.
Won a seat in Myanmar's House of Representatives (Pyithu Hluttaw) in the general election.
Served his term in Parliament, sitting on the Reform and Modernization Assessment Committee and advocating for Rohingya rights and reconciliation in Rakhine State.
The Union Election Commission barred him from running in the general election, citing alleged citizenship issues concerning his parents, who the authorities claimed were not citizens.
timeline.note: He called the ruling "illogical and ridiculous" and promised to appeal.

timeline.text: Became a board member of ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR), a founding member of the International Panel of Parliamentarians for Freedom of Religion or Belief (IPP FoRB), and President of the Arakan Institute for Peace and Human Rights (AiPAH).

people.biography:
U Shwe Maung was born on 30 June 1965 in Buthidaung, Arakan (now Rakhine State), to Rohingya Muslim parents Abdul Hadi and Aye Sein. He entered politics and won a seat in Myanmar’s House of Representatives (Pyithu Hluttaw) in the 2010 general election, becoming the only Rohingya MP in the national legislature at the time.

During his term (2011–2016), he served on the Reform and Modernization Assessment Committee and used his position to advocate for Rohingya rights and reconciliation in Rakhine State. He later became a board member of ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights (APHR), a founding member of the International Panel of Parliamentarians for Freedom of Religion or Belief (IPP FoRB), and President of the Arakan Institute for Peace and Human Rights (AiPAH).

Ahead of the 2015 general election, the Union Election Commission barred him from running. Authorities cited alleged citizenship issues concerning his parents, who they claimed were not citizens, though he stated the ruling was "illogical and ridiculous," and promised to appeal.

people.role: Social worker, politician and member of Parliament
people.epithet: Akyab's representative in the 1990 election
people.summary: A social worker and politician who was elected to represent Akyab in Burma's 1990 multi-party general election. Historical election records list him among the Muslim and Rohingya representatives elected that year, alongside those from the Maungdaw and Buthidaung constituencies.

U Shwe Yat was a social worker and politician who represented Akyab in Burma's 1990 general election. Historical election records list him among the Muslim/Rohingya representatives elected during the 1990 multi-party election.

His significance is connected to the brief restoration of Rohingya political representation during the 1990 election. Historical records list U Shwe Yat as the representative for Akyab, alongside Rohingya representatives elected from Maungdaw and Buthidaung constituencies.

people.name: U Sultan Ahmed
people.role: Parliamentary secretary and politician
people.epithet: Among the first Rohingya in Burma's legislature
people.summary: A Rohingya lawyer and politician from Maungdaw, Arakan, who was elected to the Legislature of Burma for Maungdaw in 1947, one of the first Rohingya members of the national legislature. After independence he served in the constituent assembly, was elected to the Union Parliament in 1951, 1956 and 1960, and was appointed Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Minorities with the rank of Deputy Minister. He also served on the Arakan sub-committee of the Justice Sir Ba Oo Commission on the question of Arakanese statehood.

timeline.text: Born in Thay Chaung Village (Balukhali, Maungdaw), the son of Maulana Akram Uddin.
Earned a B.A. from the University of Calcutta (1924) and a Bachelor of Law from Rangoon University (1929).
Worked as a lawyer and magistrate under the British administration, serving as Higher-Grade Pleader, Assistant Township Officer and First Class Magistrate.
Entered politics and was elected to the Legislature of Burma for Maungdaw, one of the first Rohingya members of the national legislature.
After serving in the Burmese constituent assembly following independence, he was elected to the Union Parliament in 1951, 1956 and 1960.
Appointed Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Minorities, with the rank and status of a Deputy Minister, and advocated for Rohingya rights and regional development.
Served on the Arakan sub-committee of the Justice Sir Ba Oo Commission, which recommended the creation of a Ministry of Arakan Affairs and an Arakan Affairs Council.
The military coup ended democratic governance, and with it his efforts to ensure minority inclusion in Burma's political framework.
Died on 2 March.

people.biography:
U Sultan Ahmed was a prominent Rohingya politician from Maungdaw, Arakan, and one of the longest-serving legislators from the region. Born in 1901 in Thay Chaung Village (Balukhali, Maungdaw), he was the son of Maulana Akram Uddin. He completed his education with a B.A. from the University of Calcutta (1924) and a Bachelor of Law from Rangoon University (1929), preparing him for a distinguished career in law and public service.

Ahmed began his professional life as a lawyer and magistrate, serving as Higher-Grade Pleader, Assistant Township Officer, and First Class Magistrate under the British administration. He entered politics in 1947, elected to the Legislature of Burma representing Maungdaw, becoming one of the first Rohingya members of the national legislature. After independence, he served in the Burmese constituent assembly and was repeatedly elected to the Union Parliament (1951, 1956, 1960). He was appointed Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Minorities, holding the rank and status of Deputy Minister, and played a key role in advocating for Rohingya rights and regional development.

Ahmed also contributed to the question of Arakanese statehood, serving on the Arakan sub-committee of the Justice Sir Ba Oo Commission, which recommended the creation of a Ministry of Arakan Affairs and an Arakan Affairs Council. He led efforts to ensure minority inclusion in Burma’s political framework until the 1962 military coup ended democratic governance.

U Sultan Ahmed passed away on 2 March 1981, remembered as a pioneering Rohingya leader whose work bridged his community with the national government and set a precedent for political representation in Arakan.

people.name: U Sultan Mahmud
people.role: Minister of Health and politician
people.epithet: A Rohingya voice in U Nu's cabinet
people.summary: A Rohingya politician from Sittwe (Akyab), Arakan, who served as a Member of Parliament and was appointed Minister of Health in Prime Minister U Nu's government. As a cabinet minister he worked to expand healthcare in rural areas, including the Mayu frontier townships of Buthidaung, Rathedaung and Maungdaw, and he advocated for the rights and recognition of the Rohingya and their political inclusion within the Union of Burma.

timeline.text: Born; he came from Sittwe (Akyab), Arakan.
Pursued law and became active in politics in the years after Burma's independence.

A Member of Parliament for the Arakan region, he was appointed Minister of Health in Prime Minister U Nu's government, and worked to expand healthcare and improve services in rural areas, including the Mayu frontier (Buthidaung, Rathedaung and Maungdaw townships), where many Rohingya lived.

Spoke for Arakan's Muslims in the national arena, pressing for the rights and recognition of the Rohingya and their political inclusion within the Union of Burma, and acting as a bridge between Arakan's Muslims and the central government.
Sidelined after the military coup that ended democratic governance.
Died.

people.biography:
U Sultan Mahmud was a prominent Rohingya politician from Sittwe (Akyab), Arakan, who played an important role in Burma’s parliamentary era. Born in 1919, he pursued law and became active in politics during the years following independence.

He served as a Member of Parliament representing the Arakan region and was appointed Minister of Health under Prime Minister U Nu’s government in the 1950s. As a cabinet member, he worked to expand healthcare access and improve services in rural areas, including the Mayu frontier (Buthidaung, Rathedaung and Maungdaw townships) region where many Rohingya lived.

Sultan Mahmud was also one of the most vocal Muslim leaders from Arakan in the national arena. He advocated for the rights and recognition of Rohingya communities, pushing for their political inclusion within the Union of Burma. His leadership provided a bridge between Arakan’s Muslims and the central government at a time of fragile democracy.

He continued to serve in politics through Burma’s shifting landscape but was later sidelined following the 1962 military coup that ended democratic governance. Despite this, his role as a cabinet minister remains a key part of Rohingya political history.

U Sultan Mahmud passed away in 1994, remembered as one of the highest-ranking Rohingya figures in Burma’s post-independence government.

people.name: Wai Wai Nu
people.role: Human rights activist and lawyer
people.epithet: From political prisoner to global advocate
people.summary: A Rohingya human rights activist and lawyer from Buthidaung, known for her advocacy for democracy, women's rights and justice in Myanmar. Arrested with her family at 18 while a law student, she spent nearly seven years in Insein Prison before her release in 2012, then founded the Women's Peace Network (Arakan) and Justice for Women and has spoken at the United Nations and other international forums. She has been listed in BBC 100 Women and named a TIME Next Generation Leader.
people.quote: I am not free. My community is not free. My country is not free.

timeline.text: Born in Buthidaung, Rakhine State, to Rohingya parents.
timeline.note: Her father, U Kyaw Min, was elected to Parliament in the 1990 election, but the military junta refused to recognise the results.

timeline.text: After the family moved to Yangon, she began studying law at the University of East Yangon.
Arrested with most of her family at the age of 18, in her second year of law school, and sentenced to 17 years in Insein Prison; her father received a long sentence in solitary confinement.
Released with her family under a presidential amnesty in January, after nearly seven years in prison.
timeline.note: She later said she had learned deeply from the experiences of other women detainees.

timeline.text: Completed her law degree and founded the Women's Peace Network (Arakan) and Justice for Women, working for women's rights, legal aid and peaceful coexistence between communities.
Earned a Master of Laws (LL.M.) from the University of California, Berkeley.
Listed in BBC 100 Women and named a TIME Next Generation Leader.

people.biography:
Wai Wai Nu is a Rohingya human rights activist and lawyer known for her advocacy for democracy, women’s rights, and justice in Myanmar. She was born in 1987 in Buthidaung, Rakhine State, to Rohingya parents. Her father, U Kyaw Min, was elected as a Member of Parliament in the 1990 election as a candidate of the National League for Democracy (NLD), but the military junta refused to recognize the results. She later moved to Yangon with her family and began studying law at the University of East Yangon at age 16.

In 2005, when she was 18 and in her second year of law school, Wai Wai Nu and most of her family were arrested. She was sentenced to 17 years in Insein Prison, while her father received a long sentence in solitary confinement. She spent nearly seven years in prison, where she later said she learned deeply from the experiences of other female detainees. In January 2012, her family was released under a presidential amnesty.

After her release, she completed her law degree and began human rights work. She founded Women’s Peace Network (Arakan) and Justice for Women, focusing on women’s rights, legal aid, and peaceful coexistence among communities. She has spoken at the United Nations and other international forums on human rights in Myanmar. In 2018, she earned a Master of Laws (LL.M.) from the University of California, Berkeley.

She has received international recognition, including being listed in BBC 100 Women and named a TIME Next Generation Leader. Wai Wai Nu is widely known as a Rohingya voice for human rights and justice, and her journey from political prisoner to global advocate has made her a notable figure in Rohingya activism.

people.name: Waji Ullah Arkani
people.birthplace: Chira Dan Village, Maungdaw Township, Arakan
people.role: Political activist, V-Force member and interpreter
people.epithet: From V-Force interpreter to Rohingya advocate
people.summary: A Rohingya political activist and interpreter, born in 1919 in Chira Dan Village, Maungdaw Township, who served as an interpreter with the British-organised V-Force during the Japanese occupation of Arakan. In letters to Major Anthony Irwin in 1945–46 he described discrimination against Muslims and argued for a separate Muslim territory within a constitutional framework. In 1978, as Secretary of the Arakan Historical Society, he worked to draw international attention to the plight of Rohingya refugees.

timeline.text: Born on 11 December in Chira Dan Village, Maungdaw Township. Before the Second World War he passed his matriculation examination and worked as an office clerk.
During the Japanese occupation of Arakan, joined the British-organised V-Force as an interpreter, thanks to his command of English.
timeline.note: He later studied at Calcutta University.

timeline.text: In letters to Major Anthony Irwin, described discrimination against Muslims and argued for a separate Muslim territory within a constitutional framework.
Took part in political and armed movements connected with the Rohingya question.
As Secretary of the Arakan Historical Society, worked to draw international attention to Rohingya refugees after that year's military operations.
Died.

people.biography:
Waji Ullah Arkani was a Rohingya political activist and interpreter who was born on 11 December 1919 in Chira Dan Village, Maungdaw Township. Before the Second World War, he passed his matriculation examination and worked as an office clerk. During the Japanese occupation of Arakan in 1942, he joined the British-organized V-Force and worked as an interpreter because of his command of English. He later studied at Calcutta University and became involved in Rohingya political movements.

Waji Ullah became involved in political efforts concerning the future of Muslims in Arakan. Letters he wrote to Major Anthony Irwin in 1945–46 discussed discrimination against Muslims and advocated a separate Muslim territory within a constitutional framework. After independence, he became involved in political and armed movements connected with the Rohingya question. In 1978, he served as Secretary of the Arakan Historical Society and worked to draw international attention to the condition of Rohingya refugees following the military operations of that year.
